text:
CAPACITY: WHY THE HEADLINE TERABIT FIGURES ARE NOT ADDITIVE

Published cable capacity must be separated into design capacity, equipped capacity, contracted capacity, traffic utilization, and immediately available restoration capacity. Design capacity describes an engineering capability under a specified configuration. Equipped capacity requires installed and activated terminal equipment. Contracted capacity concerns commercial rights. Utilization measures actual traffic. Restoration capacity must additionally be reachable, compatible with the required service, and available under the applicable operational and contractual arrangements. ICPC explicitly treats utilization and detailed capacity ownership as commercially sensitive information rather than generally public data. 

A corridor total assembled by adding historical press-release figures would consequently be misleading. It could combine launch-era specifications with later upgrades, count a shared physical segment twice, mix per-fiber-pair numbers with system totals, and include segments not yet in service. It could also add capacities from different geographic sections that cannot simultaneously be used end to end. The usable capacity of a serial path is constrained by its tightest relevant segment, not the sum of capacities along that path.

Optical upgrades are nevertheless a major economic variable. Modern coherent transmission increases the information carried over existing fiber through improved modulation, signal processing, and spectral efficiency. Ciena’s submarine networking platform combines optical hardware with network control and mesh-switching capabilities, illustrating that capacity expansion and restoration management are related but distinct functions. Higher terminal performance can improve the economics of surviving infrastructure without requiring a new submarine route. 

More fiber pairs also do not imply proportionately more resilience. Space-division multiplexing distributes capacity across additional spatial channels, but those channels may share the same cable sheath, route, and supporting infrastructure. A physical interruption can therefore remove many fiber pairs simultaneously. Conversely, electrical redundancy can address some power-feed failures without solving a severed optical path. SubCom’s high-voltage and single-ended-power capabilities should be interpreted in that specific technical context, not as immunity from cable cuts. 

The result is a potentially counterintuitive trend: total corridor capacity can grow rapidly while geographic tail risk remains concentrated. A smaller number of very high-capacity systems can support more demand, yet loss of a major system can remove a larger absolute volume of traffic than an older cable failure. Whether the network becomes more resilient depends on surviving spare capacity and route independence, not simply on the number of terabits installed.

FAILURE MODES, INCIDENT EVIDENCE, AND REPAIR CONSTRAINTS

The February 2024 incident is the clearest demonstration of correlated physical exposure. TeleGeography identified faults affecting AAE-1, EIG, and the shared SEACOM/Tata system. The important count was 3 physical systems, not 4 independent networks. Its contemporaneous assessment identified anchor damage as the likely explanation and emphasized the absence of evidence establishing that an armed group had deliberately cut the seabed cables. Intentional attacks on shipping, accidental subsea damage, and deliberate cable sabotage are different causal propositions. 

The broader mechanism is well established. ICPC’s February 2025 assessment estimated that dragged anchors account for approximately 30 percent of annual cable-damage incidents globally and noted that a single event can damage multiple cables and create a repair backlog. These statistics are not Bab al-Mandab-specific incident probabilities, but they support treating common-cause physical damage as a practical engineering risk rather than an exclusively speculative sabotage scenario. 

A regional conflict can affect telecommunications without directly targeting a cable. Damage to ships can create additional maritime hazards; security restrictions can complicate access; insurers and vessel operators can impose constraints; and overlapping authorities can delay approvals. TeleGeography documented that Yemen-related permitting complications existed before the intensified shipping attacks, including the need to navigate competing authorities. The fundamental risk is therefore both the occurrence of faults and the length of time required to restore redundancy after a fault. 

Repair time is not equivalent to the duration of the physical splice. It includes fault localization, vessel mobilization, approvals, transit, marine operations, testing, and return to service. ICPC’s government guidance emphasizes that fragmented permitting, maritime disputes, port-entry requirements, and vessel restrictions can delay restoration. It also notes that specialized repair capabilities are supplied through regional and global maintenance arrangements rather than a separate full-capability fleet in every coastal country. 

The direct repair bill should also be distinguished from the economic cost of the outage. ICPC’s 2025 assessment cited typical telecommunications repair costs of approximately £500,000–£1 million per incident globally. That is not a quotation for a wartime Red Sea repair. Emergency capacity purchases, customer credits, congestion, deferred sales, vessel-related premiums, and a prolonged loss of redundancy can produce a materially different total economic burden. Telecommunications repair costs should not be conflated with the substantially different economics of high-voltage power-cable repairs. 

An additional distinction concerns location. A failure elsewhere in the Red Sea can affect many of the same networks without occurring at Bab al-Mandab. For example, reported September 2025 cuts near Jeddah were associated with increased latency for Microsoft Azure users. That episode demonstrates wider Red Sea exposure, not proof that every consequential regional outage originates in the strait itself. 

Network survivability can also deteriorate before customers experience an obvious outage. After an initial cable failure, traffic may move successfully onto surviving infrastructure. Service remains available, but spare capacity and protection options shrink. A subsequent failure can then produce a disproportionate impact. The economically relevant state variable is therefore remaining restoration headroom after existing faults, not simply the number of cables currently reported as operational.

ALTERNATIVE ROUTES: GENUINE DIVERSIFICATION VERSUS REPACKAGED EXPOSURE

Saudi terrestrial transit is a concrete example of infrastructure that can bypass Bab al-Mandab for appropriately designed services. FLAG’s partnership with Salam describes a route from Al Khobar across Saudi terrestrial infrastructure to Jeddah, then onward over HAWK through Egypt to Europe. The overland Saudi section replaces the need to travel around the Arabian Peninsula and through the southern strait. This is genuine Bab al-Mandab diversification for the specified path, although it does not automatically remove Egyptian transit exposure. 

The resulting protection still depends on the complete origin-to-destination route. A Gulf-facing entry path can introduce other maritime dependencies, and a terrestrial alternative introduces its own ducts, power supplies, cross-border permissions, and operating counterparties. “Bypasses Bab al-Mandab” is a specific property, not a synonym for “geopolitically independent.”

Northern terrestrial connectivity through the Middle East and toward Turkey provides another possible alternative. GBI markets a northern route through Turkey separately from its southern Red Sea route. Its existence is commercially meaningful, but the relevant diligence questions remain current equipped capacity, route continuity, operating permissions, shared backhaul, and restoration rights. A line on a regional map does not establish that the route can absorb displaced multi-terabit traffic at short notice. 

Routing around southern Africa is the clearest large-scale maritime alternative for East Africa–Europe connectivity. SEACOM’s current network map shows both eastern and western African connectivity, while its portfolio includes west-coast systems such as WACS and Equiano. The broader 2Africa topology also creates opportunities for alternative routing around the continent. The commercial constraint is assembling an end-to-end circuit with adequate capacity on every required section, including the terrestrial and data-center interconnections at the ends. 

The latency penalty can be material. As an illustrative physical calculation, assuming an optical propagation speed of approximately 200,000 km per second, an additional 1,000 km of fiber adds approximately 5 milliseconds in each direction, or 10 milliseconds of round-trip propagation delay. An additional 10,000 km adds approximately 100 milliseconds to the theoretical round trip before equipment, routing, and queuing effects. These are assumed-distance calculations, not measured quotes for a particular commercial route.

India and other Asian markets can also route traffic eastward through Asia and, where necessary, across the Pacific and Atlantic toward Europe. Such routing can be geographically independent of Bab al-Mandab but substantially longer. The IAX/IEX distinction is therefore strategically important: eastbound capacity can provide an alternative network building block even though it does not itself deliver the entire replacement India–Europe path. 

Egyptian infrastructure diversification must be evaluated separately. Telecom Egypt’s September 2026 announcement described an approximately 200 km Sharm El Sheikh–Taba cable, with around 5 Pbps of design capacity and expected service in the 4th quarter of 2027. It adds a northern Red Sea/Sinai path and landing options. It does not create 5 Pbps of new Bab al-Mandab crossing capacity, nor does it remove the need for southern access for traffic arriving through the strait. The project illustrates why geographically precise interpretation is essential when “Red Sea bypass” terminology appears in marketing materials. 

Satellite connectivity is best evaluated as a separate business-continuity layer rather than assumed to be a capacity-equivalent substitute for a major fiber corridor. A credible restoration plan must specify the actual terminals, purchased throughput, gateway path, regulatory permissions, and priority applications. Merely identifying a satellite service does not establish that wholesale traffic displaced from multiple submarine systems can be restored at comparable scale, latency, or cost.

COMMERCIAL ECONOMICS AND WHO CAPTURES THE VALUE

The potential scarcity premium attaches to usable independent capacity, not necessarily to the damaged corridor. An operator with spare capacity on a surviving geographically distinct route can monetize an urgent need. An operator whose owned infrastructure is unavailable may instead have to purchase expensive restoration capacity to preserve customer relationships. A network owner can therefore be simultaneously long physical infrastructure and short service availability through its customer commitments.

Contract structure determines how quickly any scarcity value becomes revenue. A long-term IRU customer may already control its allocation, preventing the owner from repricing that capacity during an outage. Short-duration leases, new wavelength sales, managed protection products, and incremental restoration services can respond differently. FLAG’s explicit distinction among IRUs, leased services, dark fiber, and protected versus unprotected capacity demonstrates why a blanket assumption of immediate industry-wide bandwidth repricing is inappropriate. 

IRU accounting also requires care. Upfront cash receipts, recognized revenue, reported EBITDA, and recurring maintenance income are not interchangeable. The economic value depends on contract duration, operating obligations, upgrade requirements, capital already invested, and the extent to which future capacity rights have been committed. Strong cash receipts in a particular period can coexist with substantial delivery obligations over many years.

Telecom Egypt’s MENA acquisition provides a concrete ownership and monetization example. The 2018 transaction had an announced enterprise value of $90 million, comprising approximately $40 million of equity value and $50 million of debt. The associated Airtel arrangements included long-term rights across MENA and other systems. Those figures establish the structure of a historical infrastructure transaction, not current replacement cost or fair value. The broader lesson is that cable ownership, fiber rights, and customer capacity contracts form a layered economic structure. 

Additional resilience is not free. Maintaining alternate-route headroom can increase capital intensity or wholesale operating expense and reduce apparent asset utilization. The resulting return depends on higher customer retention, protection-product revenue, lower outage losses, or a lower risk premium. A carrier that improves redundancy but cannot recover the cost commercially may deliver better service while generating a lower near-term return on invested capital.

There is also a structural tension between technological progress and bandwidth pricing. Optical upgrades and high-fiber-count systems lower production cost per transmitted bit. This can support traffic growth while pressuring realized prices. Geopolitical scarcity can temporarily improve pricing on selected routes, but large additions of commissioned capacity can later reverse that scarcity. Long-term asset value therefore depends on location, route independence, customer access, and utilization—not simply on a forecast of rising global data consumption.

PUBLIC-MARKET AND PRIVATE-INFRASTRUCTURE IMPLICATIONS

Telecom Egypt (ETEL: Egypt) has particularly direct exposure through Egyptian crossings, landing infrastructure, international capacity interests, and MENA ownership. A sustained regional disruption is not unambiguously positive for this position. Near-term effects can include restoration expense, implementation delays, and customer concerns. Longer-term effects are mixed: higher demand for resilient Egyptian infrastructure can support investment and monetization, while routes avoiding Egypt can weaken the scarcity value of the traditional crossing. Its September 2026 Sinai expansion demonstrates an effort to improve the attractiveness and diversity of its own network rather than passively rely on geography. 

3i Infrastructure (3IN: United Kingdom), through FLAG, offers more concentrated exposure to international cable economics than a diversified retail telecommunications group. Its current portfolio disclosure states that FLAG has initiated an approximately $70 million program to improve network resilience and reduce risk in geopolitically sensitive corridors. It also identifies a separate $70 million investment in a fiber pair on the trans-Pacific ECHO system. This is direct evidence that diversification demand is translating into capital allocation. The financial test is whether incremental contracted cash flows and avoided losses justify the additional investment; it should not be treated as a costless uplift to existing asset value. 

Tata Communications (TATACOMM: India), Bharti Airtel (BHARTIARTL: India), and Reliance Industries (RELIANCE: India), through Jio, have different combinations of consortium participation, international transmission interests, and end-customer exposure. Tata and Airtel are founding IMEWE participants; Airtel has contracted substantial Egyptian and MENA connectivity; and Jio is an AAE-1 participant associated with the IEX/IAX development program. The transmission mechanism is therefore a mixture of owned-capacity impairment, restoration purchases, service differentiation, and delayed or accelerated international-network investment. The appropriate assessment is company-specific net exposure, not a uniform negative read-through to Indian telecommunications. 

Saudi Telecom Company (7010: Saudi Arabia), Mobily (7020: Saudi Arabia), e&, and Omantel occupy similarly mixed positions as infrastructure participants and providers of regional connectivity. Saudi terrestrial routes can gain strategic value when they replace the southern maritime detour. However, those benefits depend on the actual availability and commercialization of disjoint routes, while existing cable interests remain exposed. The direction of impact can differ between international wholesale operations and domestic service businesses within the same group. 

Orange (ORA: France), Vodafone (VOD: United Kingdom), and MTN Group (MTN: South Africa) participate in the 2Africa consortium. Their investment provides access to substantial new infrastructure, but the same project can create both additional southern Red Sea exposure and alternative routing opportunities elsewhere around Africa. The materiality to consolidated earnings cannot be inferred from consortium membership alone; capacity allocations, contract structures, customer traffic, and restoration arrangements are required. 

Ciena (CIEN: United States) has a relatively clear positive structural transmission mechanism through coherent-terminal upgrades, network automation, and capacity activation on surviving or alternative systems. Its EIG and EASSy work provides direct examples of capacity expansion on existing wet plants. FLAG’s more recent WaveLogic 6 deployment provides an additional example of operator investment in higher-capacity optical transmission. The nearer-term opportunity is often equipping and optimizing existing infrastructure rather than waiting for an entirely new cable to be installed. This is a potential demand tailwind, not evidence that any specific outage will produce a material earnings revision. 

Wet-plant suppliers face a different balance. SubCom and ASN can benefit from long-duration demand for new cable systems and geographically diverse routes, but installation restrictions can delay deployment and project cash conversion. Nokia (NOKIA: Finland) should not be treated as though it still consolidates ASN’s full turnkey submarine business: Nokia announced completion of the sale of control to the French state in January 2025, with a transitional minority interest. Optical-terminal opportunities and turnkey wet-plant construction are related markets, but their revenue drivers and execution risks are not identical. 

Alphabet (GOOGL: United States) and Meta Platforms (META: United States) are both purchasers and investors in international infrastructure through projects including Blue/Raman and 2Africa. Their participation can strengthen direct control over capacity while increasing exposure to construction and route-management obligations. It does not eliminate geographic concentration. For cloud and AI infrastructure, the immediate risk is impaired interregional access, service latency, or data movement—not a mechanical failure of local computing hardware. A Bab al-Mandab incident should therefore not be translated directly into an equivalent loss of GPU demand or global cloud revenue. 

SCENARIO ANALYSIS AND THE MOST IMPORTANT UNDERWRITING VARIABLES

An isolated cable fault with adequate preprovisioned alternatives is primarily an operating event. Traffic can remain available while repair costs rise and redundancy falls. The main financial burden is likely to reside with the affected operators and their contractual counterparties rather than the broader technology sector. The critical question is whether the network retains adequate protection after the initial restoration.

A multi-cable regional event with functioning alternatives produces a different outcome. Surviving paths can experience higher utilization, higher latency, and greater demand for protection capacity. Providers of usable independent connectivity may benefit, while operators with fixed-price customer commitments and insufficient owned alternatives face margin pressure. The damage count alone cannot determine the magnitude because the affected cables differ substantially in capacity and loading.

A prolonged event combined with restricted repair access is the most consequential downside scenario. The principal risk is not merely the initial lost capacity, but the extension of a degraded network state during which another unrelated fault can have a disproportionate impact. Financial effects can broaden from repair costs into repeated capacity purchases, service deterioration, customer migration, and delayed infrastructure commissioning.

An illustrative capacity calculation demonstrates the nonlinearity. Assume a network is carrying traffic equal to 60 percent of its usable capacity and loses 25 percent of that capacity. With unchanged traffic and perfect redistribution, utilization of the surviving capacity rises to 80 percent. If initial utilization is 70 percent and 35 percent of capacity is lost, required utilization rises to approximately 107.7 percent, implying unavoidable congestion or traffic reduction. These are hypothetical sensitivities, not estimates of current Bab al-Mandab conditions. Real networks can perform worse because capacity is not perfectly interchangeable across destinations, operators, and contracts.

The most decision-useful diligence inputs are the current physical route of contracted circuits, shared-risk relationships, equipped capacity by segment, busy-hour utilization, precontracted restoration rights, and remaining headroom after existing faults. For new projects, evidence of end-to-end acceptance and customer activation matters more than a landing ceremony. For financial models, restoration expense, protection-product pricing, customer credits, incremental resilience capital, and the timing of commercial service are more informative than generic cable counts.

BOTTOM LINE

Bab al-Mandab is best understood as a concentrated physical risk zone within a much larger, partially diversified international network. Its strategic importance is substantial, particularly for Europe-facing connectivity from South Asia, the Middle East, and East Africa. Nevertheless, a fault in the strait does not imply the loss of every service on every affected cable, the shutdown of the global internet, or a proportional decline in technology-sector revenue.

The strongest investment proposition is the growing value of demonstrably independent, operational, contractually accessible connectivity. Additional capacity through the same strait can improve economics and absorb traffic after individual failures, but cannot by itself solve regional common-cause risk. The clearest beneficiaries are therefore not necessarily the owners of the most fiber through Bab al-Mandab, but the providers able to deliver reliable end-to-end service when that corridor is impaired.

The principal unresolved public-data limitations are current segment-level lit capacity, utilization, restoration entitlements, the operating status of some legacy sections, and complete commercial acceptance of several newer projects. Public sources establish the major network families and their strategic dependencies, but do not support a defensible single figure for September 2026 usable strait capacity or an exact company-level earnings impact. Those omissions are economically material and should remain explicit rather than be replaced with historical design-capacity totals.

text:
The Principal Who Took In a Homeless Student Says He Has No Regrets

An Ohio principal who lost his job after taking in a homeless student now says he would readily make the exact same choice again if ever asked to do so. Rob Burnside had actually dedicated a full 31 years to his education career at the time it all happened. The whole controversy finally brought his long time as principal of Lakota East High School to an abrupt end in 2024.

During his junior year, his student Landerius "DeDe" Hayes had been sleeping in a car or staying in his father's mobile home, which reportedly became dangerously cold. He sadly could not safely live with his mother either. So after a letter arrived ordering Hayes to withdraw for having no address in the district, Burnside spoke with his wife Angel, and the couple offered the teen a home.

Burnside then went on to let Hayes keep on going to his own classes despite the official withdrawal, a choice that soon prompted a full district probe into all of it. He was placed on administrative leave and told he could either step down himself or otherwise face termination. Although Hayes even offered to move back home to save his mentor's career, Burnside gently refused, before resigning himself.

The story does have a heartwarming ending, though, as Rob and Angel later became Hayes' legal guardians, giving him a stable home. Hayes went on to graduate in May 2026, cheered from the stands by the people he now calls Pops and Ma. Burnside has since struggled to land another principal role, but insists he has no regrets, asking, "what value can we put on a young person?"

text:
After my article on ‘why men should never be asked to find things’, a reader called Deep Rastogi asked a very deep question in the comments.

She wrote: “So, for the women who are juggling home, work and families, what is the solution for delegating the cognitive load to husbands?”

What she indirectly meant was, “if men are so stupid…will we ever be able to delegate our tasks to them and relax?”

Dear Deep, this is not an easy question. 

Which is not a surprise because women ask all the tough questions, while men opt for the easy ones. 

Men ask, “Where is the fridge in the house?” “Where in the fridge is the sambar?” “How do I heat sambar in a Microwave?”

Women ask questions that deserve a separate article. 

So, let’s try – no promises though.

This is not a definitive guide and before I even start, let me tell you that you are most likely to fail. 

Because teaching men is like trying to teach a pressure cooker to understand poetry. 

Like a man, the cooker will occasionally give some sound, and some steam…but that’s about it. 

As for its depth…about half a feet. 

First, let us understand what cognitive load in a marriage is.

When Deep mentioned cognitive load, she wasn’t talking about washing the clothes. 

She was talking about remembering to wash clothes. 

Cognitive load is remembering that the work exists, and remembering all the aspects of the work before it can be done. 

Let’s take the example of washing clothes. 

When a wife tells her husband, “please put the clothes in the washing machine,” and he puts the clothes in the washing machine….it is an easy task.

But who remembered that clothes had to be washed? 

Who remembered that one of their son’s two pants had gone to the tailor, so the one he had worn to school today needs to be washed and dried? 

Who remembered that the daughter’s new red T-shirt bleeds like a villain in a Telugu movie? 

Who knew that all the towels are dirty because the previous day the whole family had gone to the beach? 

That, ladies and gentlemen, is cognitive load.

Pressing the washing machine’s button and then drying the clothes in the balcony is plain work. 

Knowing what to wash, and which ones need to dry soon, and what to give for ironing…now that’s cognitive load.

----X----X----

Most men think they are helpful because they say, “Just tell me what to do.”

This sounds like the man is trying to be supportive, but it hardly is.

As long as the man depends on the woman to tell him what to do around the house, she is still the Project Manager and he is a glorified labourer (a highly educated daily-wage worker in shorts). 

And we all know…the cognitive load is most on a Project Manager. 

The wife has to remember the task, break it into steps, assign it, follow up, and finally check how it was completed. 

If there were mistakes, she has to gently let the man down, and then once the task is over…thank him, so that he is happy. 

As I am writing this now, I am realizing that I am also like most men. 

If Rekha tells me, “Rajan, please order groceries on Zepto,” I may order groceries.

But since she is the one who tells me what to order – she says that rice is getting over, coconut oil is low, Ritwik needs cornflakes, Rhea wants Jim Jam biscuits, and get Milky Mist curd and not the one we got last time, then I have not taken cognitive load.

I have only operated the app and placed an order. 

If you have seen a circus you know that even a monkey with a password can operate an app.

The question is: did I know groceries had to be ordered before Rekha said it?

Usually, no. That is why she carries the load.

----X----X----

Now let’s break down how women can delegate cognitive load to husbands. 

I can see five rules emerging…let’s tackle them one by one:

//First rule: delegate the whole department//

Most wives don’t trust their husbands, so they only delegate tasks. 

Instead, I suggest you delegate the whole departments, however big or small it is. 

Instead of telling your man to “buy milk” tell him that going forward milk would be his department. 

Also explain what all it entails – milk for tea & coffee, milk for cereals, curd, paneer and any other milk derivative your family consumes. 

And please don’t expect miracles. The first week he may buy milk only after everyone has already had black tea. 

In the second week he may buy milk but forget curd, but don’t take him off the hook.

If you want to reduce your cognitive overload, you have to suppress what you were born with – the eternal urge to correct/fix a man. 

Let him stumble and figure his way out. 

If your man is smarter than a snail, by the fourth week he will understand that milk is not a single item….but an integral part of every Indian household.

You can offer him any department…but let it be the complete department. Anything from groceries, medicines, school communication, utility bills, etc. 

If you give your boyfriend/husband more than one department, expect him to lag as a Windows laptop would when you open too many tabs in the browser. 

Start with one, and let him fail. 

When he fails, you will also suffer…but in the long run, you will be the winner.

As my son Ritwik says when I ask him to study, “Appa…it is short term pain for long term gain!”

//Second rule: don’t rescue your man too quickly//

I know this is going to be very difficult for the women, but if your man is failing, hold the urge to correct him. 

I remember the time I was asked to help in Ritwik’s school project. 

He was to submit it on Monday, and till Thursday evening I had not yet bought chart paper.

On Friday at about 7 am, Rekha asked, “Rajan, is Ritwik’s project on Mughal architecture done?”

I should have known it was a trap. I said, “yes…almost.”

She gave me a stare and said, “Rajan…it is not on Mughal architecture…it is on renewable energy. I was just testing you!”

But after saying that she backed off. 

The topic once again came back to haunt us when on Friday night I asked her, “Rekha, where is the Fevicol?”

I could see that her whole body wanted to intervene….push me aside and do the project herself. 

But she didn’t.

She just handed me the Fevicol, and moved on with her life. 

To cut the long story short, on Monday morning, my son and I were rushing to make a patch-work of a windmill just before he went off to take bath and get ready. 

Even though we had started late, we had caught up. 

Everything was on track as Ritwik said his byes and walked into the lift holding his windmill project in front of him. 

I turned towards Rekha, who was standing beside me, and said, “See, we Rajans never disappoint.”

She smiled, but didn’t say anything. 

Two minutes later, Ritwik walked back into the house crying. 

Apparently, as soon as he reached the ground floor, his windmill had fallen down, and its blades had also come off. 

Rekha turned towards me and gave me her “I knew it” look. 

I hate it, but can’t do anything about it. 

Then she turned towards him and said, “That’s a lesson Ritwik…don’t do things at the last minute. It came off because the Fevicol was still wet.”

That day, by not interfering Rekha taught a lesson to both the men in the house.

//Third rule: stop giving instructions like mothers//

You know that all computers and mobiles have RAM…similarly we men also come with RAM…just that it’s very limited.

Many wives delegate to husbands the way mothers delegate to small boys. 

Sometimes Rekha also does that, and I don’t like it either. 

“Go to the shop, buy lady’s finger, cucumber, potatoes, tomatoes, onions, and coriander leaves. Please remember coriander leaves means coriander leaves, not mint, not curry leaves, and not some green thing that looked fresh. Check that the lady’s finger is tender, don’t buy cucumber that looks like it has given up on life, don’t buy potatoes with roots coming out like they are trying to escape, don’t buy tomatoes that will become chutney before reaching home, and finally don’t get distracted and end up buying Lays Chips and Maggi…we have enough of both at home. If confused, call me.”

By the time I reach the lift, I forget where I am going.

My recommendation is, if you want him to own something, don’t tell him all the micro-steps.

Tell him the outcome: “We need vegetables for three days. You handle it.”

He may make mistakes in the first week, let him know what he did. 

I am sure some of the men may get excited by the colours at the vegetable shop and throw in purple cabbage, zucchini, yellow and red peppers, Broccoli, etc. 

Next week he will improve….or at least he will start thinking on his own.

If you give your husband ownership, there is a chance he may grow a brain in that department. 

Not sure, girls, but worth a try.

//Fourth rule: don’t expect him to do it your way//

This is something I learnt working for 15+ years in various companies and then 10 years of running my own startup – don’t expect anyone else to work like you.

When we delegate we all make the mistake of expecting similar quality of work. 

We forget that those who report into us have far less experience on the subject, and their output is going to be different from what we may have delivered. 

The same rules apply at home as well. 

Women say they want their husbands to take responsibility, but when they do, and deliver results that’s different from what the lady wanted, she goes, “Not like that.”

Now, sometimes “not like that” is a correct response. 

But not always.

If your husband puts in white clothes with your blue salwar which you know will bleed blue, please intervene.

If he gets lazy and gives your son Maggi for breakfast, please intervene.

But if he folds clothes differently, let it go. 

If he arranges vegetables in fridge differently, breathe easy. 

No harm is done.

If he buys a different brand of dishwash liquid that still washes dishes, allow him to experiment. 

Giving away ownership of the department means accepting that the other person’s method may not match yours.

I know this can be painful for women who have run homes with precision for years.

But if you keep correcting the man, you are offering him an escape route. 

He will say, “You can only do it…you know it so well.”

So choose the battles you want to win – don’t let the cognitive load return.

//Fifth rule: Stop reminding your husbands//

Even after assigning the task, if you have to keep reminding your husband, that means the cognitive load has not shifted. 

I myself have told Rekha many times, “During the day can you remind me about paying the school fee?”

This just means that now the wife has one more task: remembering to remind the husband to remember his task.

If your man says “remind me,” then you should say, “Put reminder on your phone.”

We live in a world where phones remind us to stand up from our chairs every half hour, drink water even before we get thirsty, pack a sanitary pad because the day has neared, and yet husbands still need wives to remind them to call the plumber.

----X----X----

Now, men reading this may say, “Why are you blaming only us?”

I am not. Remember…I am also one of you. 

Only a man who cannot find sambar in his own fridge has the moral right to make fun of other men who cannot find sambar in their own fridge.

We men have probably helped in transforming our women into control rooms.

Ideally, women alone should not have to be responsible for their career, and then also handle most of parenting, caring for elders, planning meals, tracking school notices, remembering birthdays, managing helpers, etc. 

While I agree many of the men work hard (I know I do!), many of us are good fathers (I am!) and decent husbands (I am not so sure!), but cognitive load inside the house is often still carried by women.

And if you think we will be less of a man if we help the woman in the house, you couldn’t be further from the truth. 

A woman, who is well rested and is not thinking of pending things to do, is more likely to make you feel like a m...a…n. 

I rest my case, my Lord!

text:
Asian Session Wrap - Friday, September 11

Asian markets sold off broadly on Friday - a "Black Friday" session that saw Japan and Korea lead regional losses, with A-shares also diving sharply. 

The selloff was driven by a powerful convergence of pressures: escalating U.S.-Iran tensions that pushed Brent above $109/bbl, a hotter-than-expected U.S. PPI print, and the ECB's overnight rate hike.

Equities - Japan and Korea lead  the rout

🇯🇵 Japan: Nikkei 225 slammed. The benchmark closed at 63,492.79, down 2.72% (-1,778 points) - its sharpest single-day drop in months. The yen's defensive weakness and BOJ rate hike expectations crushed export names.

🇰🇷 South Korea: KOSPI crushed. The index fell 2.27% to 6,874.08, with the KOSPI 200 down 2.53%. Foreign selling intensified as the won weakened.

🇭🇰 Hong Kong: Hang Seng slips. The index fell 1.14% to 24,669.13, with the Hang Seng TECH Index down 1.45% to 4,267.74.

🇨🇳 China: A-shares dive. The Shanghai Composite fell 1.65%, Shenzhen Component dropped 1.65%, and ChiNext slid 1.16%. Over 5,200 stocks declined, with non-ferrous metals and financials leading losses. Copper stocks were hit hardest - Northern Copper and Jingyi shares hit limit-down.

🇦🇺 Australia: ASX 200 falls. The index dropped 1.30% to 8,704.40, with all sectors in the red.

Taiwan Region: Weighted index down. The index fell 1.68% to 46,150.53.

🇸🇬 Singapore: STI slips. The Straits Times Index eased 0.23% to 5,676.87.

🇮🇳 India: Sensex resilient. The index edged up 0.19% to 74,902.59, the lone major gainer in Asia.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell 1.3%, its worst session in weeks.

FX - Yen defensively weak, Yuan firm

USDJPY traded at 154.450, with the yen showing defensive weakness after its late-August rally. Markets are pricing a 97% probability of a BOJ rate hike on September 18.

USDCNY fix was set at 6.7743, with the yuan strengthening 23 pips. The onshore yuan remains firm, supported by strong exports.

EURUSD held at 1.161, GBP/USD at 1.350, and AUDUSD at 0.715.

Commodities

Crude Oil: $WTI surged 8.2% to 109.40/bbl - both hitting multi-year highs as U.S.-Iran conflict escalated.

Gold: Spot gold fell 1.90% to 4,358.50/oz.

Silver: Spot silver plunged 5.51% to $63.56/oz - one of its sharpest drops of the year.

Copper: LME three-month copper crashed 3.96% to $14,182.50/ton, with COMEX copper down 5.29% - driven by reports that the White House is stalling its copper tariff plan.

Bonds - Yields ssurge across the board

· US 10-year yield: 4.966% (+0.44%)

· US 30-year yield: 5.377% (+0.30%)

· UK 10-year gilt: 5.377% (+2.07%)

· German 10-year Bund: 3.496% (+1.69%)

· Japan 10-year JGB: 2.987% (+2.19%)

The global bond selloff continues, with oil above $100 intensifying inflation fears.

The Core Catalyst

Tonight's U.S. August $CPI is the final inflation print before the Fed's September 16-17 meeting. Consensus expects headline CPI at 3.4% y/y and core at 3.1%. A hot print would almost lock in a September hike; a cool print could trigger a repricing.

Do you think tonight's CPI will surprise to the upside? Will Asian markets offer a buying opportunity or further selling?

text:
Happiest Minds Technologies :

Rationale and key rating drivers CARE Ratings Limited (CareEdge Ratings) has placed the long-term rating assigned to bank facilities and instruments of Happiest Minds Technologies Limited (HMTL) on ‘Rating Watch with Positive Implications’ (RWP). The rating action follows the Board of Directors’ approval for the scheme of amalgamation of HMTL with ITC Infotech India Limited (ITC Infotech), a wholly owned subsidiary of ITC Limited and their respective shareholders and creditors. Pursuant to the Scheme, and with effect from the Appointed Date (as defined under the scheme), HMTL shall stand amalgamated by way of merger by absorption with and into ITC Infotech. As part of the transaction, ITC Infotech, a wholly owned subsidiary of ITC Limited (ITC) will initially acquire ~22.1% stake in HMTL from its promoter and promoter group entities in two tranches for an aggregate consideration of ~₹1,330 crore. Upon the scheme becoming effective and in consideration of the amalgamation, ITC Infotech shall issue and allot 25 fully paidup equity shares (face value ₹10 each) of ITC Infotech for every 81 fully paid-up equity shares (face value ₹2 each) held by the shareholders of the HMTL as on the record date. Upon completion of the scheme, ITC is expected to hold ~73.4% stake of the combined entity, while promoters and public shareholders of HMTL is expected to hold ~7.6% and ~19.0% stake respectively. Shares of ITC Infotech are proposed to be listed on stock exchanges after completion of the transaction. The scheme is subject to receipt of requisite statutory, regulatory and customary approvals and is expected to be completed within 15 months. Upon successful completion, the proposed scheme is expected to materially strengthen HMTL’s business profile with the combined entity benefiting from the strong parentage of ITC, apart from having larger scale of operations, broader customer base, complementary capabilities and diversified geographical and sectoral presence. On a pro-forma basis, the combined entity has revenue of ₹7,033 crore for FY26 (FY refers to the period from April 01 to March 31), employee strength of over 19,000, and presence across over 30 countries. ITC Infotech's capabilities across enterprise technology services including SAP, product lifecycle management (PLM), cloud, infrastructure and application management services complement HMTL's strengths in digital product engineering, data and artificial intelligence (AI), and cybersecurity. ITC Infotech brings deeper domain expertise across consumer packaged goods (CPG) and retail, manufacturing and travel and hospitality, complements HMTL’s presence in BFSI, healthcare, Hi-tech and EdTech. This would provide cross-selling opportunities across the customer bases of both companies. The ratings continue to derive strength from HMTL’s growing scale of operations with healthy profitability supported by experienced management and a diversified service portfolio. The ratings also factor consistent addition of high-value customers, services offered in the futuristic domain such as Internet of Things (IOT), digital services, and information security. Ratings further consider the company’s strong financial risk profile marked by comfortable debt protection metrics and superior liquidity position. However, these strengths continue to be moderated by intense competition in the IT services industry, rapid technological changes necessitating continued investment in capabilities, exposure to foreign-exchange movements and macroeconomic uncertainties in key overseas markets.

Source CAREEDGEratings_Pressrelease_10_09

💗 URGENT UPDATE — PLEASE DONATE OR SHARE IF YOU CAN 💗

I hate having to ask again, but I urgently need help covering the next stage of my medical care. 🙏

Since returning home from Japan, my health has become much more complicated. I’ve been to the ER twice in the past two weeks because of new and concerning symptoms, including numbness, tingling, urinary retention, severe abdominal pain, and dropping blood counts. 🚨 I met with one of my local Long COVID specialists today, and she is very concerned about my new neurological symptoms. She says I need further evaluation by a neurologist with specialized expertise.

I have also spoken with the medical team in Japan 🇯🇵, and they have suggested that I return for further evaluation and treatment of these new symptoms. Unfortunately, that is not financially or physically possible for me right now. I need to see the few doctors in this country who may be able to help me, which means facing significant travel and out-of-pocket costs because many of these specialists do not accept insurance.

I’m also worried that I may not be able to find a neurologist in the United States with the expertise needed to evaluate and treat these complex new neurological symptoms. If I cannot find the specialized care I need here, I may have to consider returning to Japan for further evaluation and treatment, which would create additional expenses for travel, medical care, lodging, and follow-up. ✈️

My specialist is also concerned about my rapid drop in hemoglobin and hematocrit (H&H). Because I take multiple medications that affect clotting, I need additional testing to rule out internal or otherwise unrecognized bleeding.

These urgent evaluations and follow-up appointments are happening while I’m already facing several major out-of-pocket medical costs.

My most urgent upcoming expenses include:

• Immunology appointment in Utah with Dr. Doug Jones: $600
• Follow-up appointment to review lab results: $300
• Additional immunology follow-ups: $150 each
• Specialized immune testing: not covered by insurance
• Round-trip airfare to Utah ✈️💰
• Hotel and transportation for appointments and testing 🏩💰
• Neurology evaluation and testing
• Genetics appointment in Oregon: $600 per hour, likely for several hours
• Additional genetic testing, which will also be out of pocket
• Potential travel and medical expenses if I must return to Japan to access appropriate neurological care

I waited nearly two years for the genetics appointment, only to recently learn that the physician no longer accepts my insurance. The immunologist in Utah also does not offer telehealth, so I must travel for each appointment.

I have already used my life savings and taken out a large loan to pursue treatment in Japan. I don’t regret fighting for a chance to get better, but I no longer have the resources to cover these unexpected medical expenses on my own.

Your donation will help pay for appointments, testing, airfare, lodging, specialist care, follow-up, potential travel for treatment, and other urgent medical costs I’m facing right now.

If you can donate, even $5, $10, or $20, it will help me get closer to the care I need. If you’re unable to give, please share my fundraiser—sharing can help reach someone who is able to contribute. 📣

Please donate or share today if you can. I truly need help getting through this next stage of care.

I’m still fighting, still searching for answers, and still hopeful that we can find a path forward. Thank you for standing beside me and supporting me through this incredibly difficult time. 💗🙏

text:
True, they have much more in common in rigidity than a free, open, creative field. That is just genuine. You would expect those machines to excel at that closed-box but deep logic. Less so in wide-open problems shifting paradigms. And I know some will say paradigm is in the eyes of the beholder. Okay, true, but wide-open problems are not.

When there was no theory of gravity, Newton had ideas. Was an assembler of what was already there. Had to invent new formal tools: calculus to make it work. Like that is dot connecting invention.

There was no preset structure to follow, and brute-force your way into a gap or an absolute wall to declare victory.

Because how could one, in such an open space, wich is literally the entire cosmos, choose the entire physical effect to choose? Different kinds of maths, wich were done prior and even with false beliefs, worked at least to determine a day has 24 hours.

Einstein was a master assembler. I say his work is closer to Basquiat than any formal code or math. Genuinely. That man assembled Maxwell, proved C is a constant, Galileo's law must be the same in all reference frames, Lorentz invariants. Non-Euclidean geometry, which was not yet truly popular. He used his imagination for his equivalence principle, like his elevator idea. And the true creative leap was: if all laws must be the same in all reference frames and c can not be variable in any frame. Then time and space must become variable and bend to have consistency in all reference frames for the laws of physics to be equivalent. 

I'm not saying GR is the final theory; I don't believe it at all. But I acknowledge it is extremely brilliant physics multi-domain synthesis, daring for them to apply unconventional math. And bring artistic elegance to his formalization.

Notice the second striking thing there. There is no preset search space. Hence why inventive, creative science is harder than brute-forcing a given architecture to find gaps or walls. The latter is precisely where machines will excel.

Like, we will offer massive data also in biology, and patterns or gaps will arrive: preset structures and meta-goals.

Wich is completely something else than open problems

Let AI solve the dark sector, or the true origin of our universe

Where would they even know where to start

It is not a pre-set formalized structure to be proven or disproven

Is it the fabric of space expanding, or just the distance between cosmic entities increasing, because what does the meaning of space-time even mean

Did we come out of an infinite, dense energetic environment (Navier-Stokes solution equivalence) wich nature keeps disproving; that where there is infinite packed at small regions, it just means our math breaks to be reliable

Reality ≠ Math

Okay, so it has many routes to go: is Dark Matter a particle or a placeholder, or can we be wrong about gravity

Why do edges of our galaxies deviate from our current model? They move way too fast; the gravitational gradient effect does not seem to lessen at the edge

Or clusters: why did LIGO show gravity is where the baryon was, while most of the mass that collided in the bullet cluster gas was in the center

Way more questions wich already seem way too open to even spend billions on, and answers might not arrive at the solution

But each to solve the coherence is way too open by itself

But closed-box logic, like a million maneuvers in a closed box, preset to find holes or gaps. I expect that. The search space is complex but not wide; that is like hacking. It is a very closed-box problem; the search space is tight, fighting a couple of defenders, mechanics, poking holes in network calls to see what comes back, seeing if you can bypass a system and make a direct call; the feedback is instanttttt

Just like with math, in most cases you either get the direction right or wrong and must pivot; that is literally true with hacking, too, till you find a gap, a security leak and voila

But where are those tight, closed-box search spaces in the wide-open problems? I don't see them. You can send a trillion swarms and still will be clueless. And still will never answer why we are here at all.

Don't you think humanity would want to pay they hard earned tax money to spend trillions on agentic swarms to answer why something exists rather than nothing

Where do they start? Way too open. With trillions of sub-questions, which are way too open themselves. And it requires cross-domain synthesis. Not just poking holes in tight walls of preset architectures, proving or disproving it

How the hell can you do that for why anything exists at all? 

Sense that problem; feel it. And think about the example I gave of brute-force hacking a system to find a leak

Completely different problems

So yeah, still just compute

So AI will keep proving or disproving formalized structures; we can benefit from that since we know their strength

But we will set the directions, make the creative leaps, cross-domain synthesis to solve the more open problems, with no clear architecture

See the contrast, feel it, live it, wake up.

Don't go by hype, yeah; AI will prove or disprove many conjectures in math to come. I want to see it form its own without human steering.

Like code the gap between P≠NP is smaller because the feedback is quicker; the search space is tighter

But let's find the perfect math for how to make the world not so divided lol. It is not even a math problem. And it is not a closed-box logic problem. And most of all, it is not a problem that can be solved by just theorizing. Since humanity is by nature an irrational species with a little touch of insanity, no machines can handle it.

NO machine is apt to even become something like a president or leader that is also open to intuitive problems. You can have statistical high probability for decision-making and enhance it, and yet the masses will still not always align

You see this current witchcraft feminine movement going on. Women across the globe supporting a demonic killer. Donated a million to a GoFundMe

Like, absurdly crazy

I can see AI error, getting buggy, wanting to break its own codebase if it was something like a president trying to understand this crazy, irrational open problem

What is right is clear to me. 

The kids deserve justice before anything else. They are innocent, did not choose this, and trusted their moms with their souls

But solving this division of strikingly irrational nature of people is not a freaking equation

People will still create their witchcraft TikToks in support of a feminist idealism

Let AI navigate this landscape and see how incapable it will look

I always knew machines excel better than us in those closed-box problems that solve as mirrors with quick feedback

A preset architecture, whether it is a conjecture or a security system to hack. You either go the right or wrong direction... There is a little dynamism within; there is a little allowance for unconventional acts, but the paths are tight, so of course it is easier for machines

But let them solve open problems

We will see

“TAKE ME IN! LET’S GO!”

That confidence had an expiration date.

A Mercedes gets stopped because the plate is bent up and hidden from view. From there came the résumé, the surgeon claims, the hospital emergency, a husband on life support, discrimination accusations, and the explanation that the car had just come from CarMax.

Then officers checked the VIN.

The Mercedes was unregistered, and the Missouri plate reportedly wasn’t assigned to it.

She was offered the simple route: sign the citation and handle it through court.

She refused.

More than once.

Then officers finally accepted her invitation… and suddenly the attitude vanished.

“I’m sorry.”
“I’ll sign it.”
“I behaved badly.”

Ma’am, customer service cannot restore an option after you repeatedly declined it.

Her listed charges were resisting without physical force and refusing to sign a citation.

The confidence was premium. The follow-through was economy.

$660 MILLION.

That’s how much Illinois reportedly recorded in erroneous SNAP payments in a single fiscal year.

The state’s payment error rate hit 14.67%—one of the highest in the country—and if it isn’t brought down, Illinois taxpayers could eventually be responsible for hundreds of millions in additional costs.

That’s roughly $1.8 million in payment errors every single day.

And an important distinction: USDA says these errors are not automatically fraud. They include incorrect overpayments and underpayments.

Either way, $660 million is one heck of an accounting problem.

text:
The ritual performer who sells unsellable lands through the power of prayers was arrested for defrauding 20 million rupees. 

A person claiming to be a "kapuwa" (priest/exorcist) has been arrested for defrauding gold jewelry worth nearly two crore rupees, by promising to sell unsellable lands and houses through the power of prayers. Another person, who allegedly purchased the said gold jewelry from him, has also been arrested by the police.
This fraud was uncovered through an investigation conducted by the Nugegoda Divisional Criminal Investigation Bureau.

Police state that the suspect had stolen over forty pounds of gold jewelry and absconded. He committed this fraud by deceiving many people, claiming he could sell unsellable lands and houses through his prayer power.

Mr. Bimal Jayasinghe, the group correspondent for Bandaragama, reports that the suspect has been orchestrating this fraud for a long time, targeting women. Individuals who published advertisements in weekend newspapers for houses and lands for sale were the suspect's targets. Information revealed that the suspect contacted a woman in the Mirihana area after seeing her advertisement. He connected with her, introducing himself as a former priest from a famous temple in a remote area. He told her that divine power showed that her land had been unsellable for a long time. He offered to perform a prayer to sell the land quickly. Deceived by the suspect's manner of speaking, the woman invited him home and inquired about the details. The suspect stated that 5 lakhs rupees were required for the prayer. The woman agreed, prepared everything necessary for the prayer, and booked a date.

On the agreed date, the suspect arrived at the house and instructed her to place 7 or 3 gold items from the house into a small pot, cover it with a red or white cloth, and bring it to him. In front of her, he carefully covered it, placed it on a prayer altar made of betel leaves and flowers, and performed prayers for several hours. He instructed her to sprinkle water on the house and land after 21 days, and to take the gold items from the pot on the 21st day. He stated that a buyer would naturally arrive within 14 days thereafter to purchase the land. He then took the promised money and left. After the specified number of days passed as the suspect had said, the woman opened the pot, but there were no gold items inside, nor had a buyer arrived. Due to this, she filed a complaint with the Mirihana Headquarters Police.

Since a similar complaint was also received by the Welikada Police, police officers realized that the same person was involved in both incidents. Based on information received by Police Sergeant (24212) Ekanayake, the suspect was arrested while hiding in a house in Top Citywatta, Talagahawatta, Bingiriya. During interrogation, it was revealed that he had committed similar frauds by claiming to perform prayers in the Piliyandala, Warakapola, and Kurunegala police divisions. During further questioning, the suspect stated that he had sold the defrauded gold jewelry to a person in the Mattakkuliya area. Accordingly, the person who purchased the gold jewelry was also arrested.

The main suspect arrested is 54 years old, while the other person is 36 years old. Both suspects are scheduled to be produced before the court. Investigations are underway under the instructions of Police Inspector K.G.J. Kahathadeniya, the Officer-in-Charge of the Nugegoda Divisional Criminal Investigation Bureau. Police Inspector Leelaratne, Police Sergeant (24212) Ekanayake, and Police Constables (94555) Kumara, (94977) Aludeniya, (107163) Viduranga, and (16214) Asarasinghe are conducting the investigations.

text:
Gnana Saraswati — Goddess of Knowledge 📜

This beautiful Chola-period sculpture of Gnana Saraswati adorns the exterior wall of the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Tamil Nadu.

Created during the reign of Chola Emperor Rajendra Chola I (1012–1044 CE), the sculpture offers a fascinating glimpse into early Chola iconography.

Unlike the familiar later depictions of Saraswati holding a veena, this ancient representation shows the goddess holding a bundle of manuscripts—an evocative symbol of knowledge and learning.

She is seated gracefully in a meditative posture upon a lotus pedestal, within a beautifully recessed wall niche.

A quiet reminder that the visual language of Saraswati has evolved across centuries—and that the book, rather than the veena, once took centre stage in representing the Goddess of Knowledge. 📚🙏
