text:
🌍🧭 Around the World in 80 Clubs: A Journey Through the Weird, Wacky and Wonderful World of Football

The beautiful game is played everywhere, but sometimes the sheer logistics of getting 22 players onto a pitch defy all common sense. From 10,000-mile-away days to playing on moving ferries, here are 20 of the most absurd stories in football by @paul_c_watson who has literally written the book on it

🏝️ 1. Shipwrecked Football
When Chilean side Santiago Wanderers drew a trip to the Juan Fernández Islands in the 2024 Copa Chile, they faced a minor issue: no commercial flights.

To reach Robinson Crusoe Island—400 miles off the coast—they had to hitch a ride on the Chilean Navy supply ship, Aquiles. Their opposition? A hastily assembled team of local fishermen, slightly hampered by players missing training due to lobster harvesting. The locals put up an almighty fight, narrowly losing 2-1.

🗑️ 2. The Worst Team in History?
When a club gets kicked out of a league, you usually assume they cheated. For Spanish side Sueca United, it was the exact opposite: they were expelled for being too bad.

Set up as a haven for anyone who couldn't get a game elsewhere, they lost over 300 games in a row across 11 seasons, conceding more than 4,000 goals (an average scoreline of 24-0). In September 2023, the Valencian Football Federation finally lost patience and threw them out after a 40-0 defeat.

⛴️ 3. A Derby on a Ferry
The Estonian islands of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa have a fierce rivalry, but when they scheduled a derby in 2013, neither surrendered home advantage.

The solution? They laid down a grass lawn on the deck of the M/S Muhumaa passenger ferry and played a 5-a-side match at sea. Hiiumaa won 4-1—luckily, without anyone taking a tackle over the railing.

🧳 4. The Ultimate Groundhoppers
Sudanese giant Al Hilal recently pulled off an unprecedented feat: winning the league in three different countries in just two seasons.

Displaced by civil war, they joined Mauritania's top tier in 2024-25 (finishing top as 'honorary champions'), returned briefly to Sudan to win the short-form Elite League, and then joined the Rwanda Premier League for 2025-26, winning that too.

🏔️ 5. Oxygen Masks Required
You think playing in La Paz is hard? Try a visit to Peruvian side Unión Minas.

Their Estadio Daniel Alcides Carrión sits at 13,973 feet above sea level—less than 4,000 feet lower than Mount Everest base camp. Away teams were routinely so incapacitated by the thin air that oxygen masks were a permanent fixture in the away dressing room at half-time.

⚰️ 6. Six Titles and a Funeral
Maltese side Valletta FC don't just win trophies (including an incredible domestic sextuple in 2000-01)—they torment their rivals while doing it.

Whenever Valletta win the league, fans hold a mock funeral street parade through the capital, carrying coffins branded with the crests of beaten opponents. Needless to say, when they suffered their first-ever relegation in 2023-24, rival fans didn't hold back the celebrations.

🌴 7. A 10,000-Mile Away Day
Since 1961, the Coupe de France has allowed overseas French territories to enter.

In 2024-25, fourth-tier Normandy side US Avranches drew AS Dragon... from Papeete, Tahiti. The squad traded rainy northern France for a 10,000-mile trip to a Pacific paradise. The downside? They lost on penalties after a 2-2 draw.

🤦‍♂️ 8. The Wrong Team Entirely
When former West Brom winger Thievy Bifouma signed for Iranian side Esteghlal Khuzestan in 2024, he admitted he only joined so he could play against Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr in the Asian Champions League.

The snag? Al Nassr were actually playing Esteghlal FC—a completely different club based hundreds of miles north in Tehran. Bifouma only realised when his friend Gael Kakuta called him asking why he wasn't at Esteghlal FC's training ground.

🔒 9. Locked Out of Away Games
Welsh side HMP Prescoed compete in Gwent League Division Two, but their squad isn't made of guards—they're inmates at an open prison.

Because they aren't allowed to leave for away fixtures, they must forfeit every away match 5-0 and take a three-point deduction. The absolute mathematical maximum they can score in a season is zero points. They finished last season on -5.

🚌 10. The American Nightmare
When Caribbean side Antigua Barracuda joined the US third tier, financial collapse forced them to relocate entirely to the US mainland for their 2013 season.

Living in a cramped Tampa hotel, they travelled up to 10 hours in a tiny minibus for matches and frequently had to train in the hotel car park. They played 26, lost 26.

💩 11. Disgustingly Cute Sponsors
Japanese J3 League side FC Ryukyu hail from Okinawa, requiring a 400+ mile journey for every single away game.

To make matters stranger, they turned heads by signing the 'Unko Museum' as their back-of-shirt sponsor—an interactive museum in Japan dedicated entirely to the theme of poop.

🌶️ 12. Itching to Get Home
After a heated match in Benin, players from Bani Ganse boarded their coach for a 10-hour drive home, only to start itching uncontrollably.

Rival Loto-Popo fans had sprayed industrial itching powder all over the bus seats after believing Bani Ganse had used 'suspicious substances' on the pitch.

✈️ 13. A 9,000-Mile Commute
When Baltika Kaliningrad were promoted to the Russian top tier in 2023, no one celebrated harder than SKA-Khabarovsk.

Khabarovsk (near China) and Kaliningrad (an enclave on the Baltic Sea) are separated by a gruelling 9,000-mile round trip—meaning Khabarovsk clock up around 70,000 miles of travel per season.

🇸🇨 14. The Wrong Andy Morrison
In 2010, youth coach Andrew Amers-Morrison went on holiday to the Seychelles. The local FA mistakenly believed he was former Manchester City captain Andy Morrison and offered him the national team job on the spot.

He accepted, but the ruse unravelled when a journalist called the actual Andy Morrison to ask about his tactical plans for the Seychelles.

⛵ 15. Abandon Ship!
On the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena, local side Crystal Rangers suffered eye-watering 36-0 and 30-0 defeats in 2020.

The context? On both occasions, they could only field eight players because an emergency rescue at sea forced several squad members to sprint for the lifeboats right before kick-off.

🚁 16. Flying by Helicopter to Africa
AD Ceuta are a Spanish side based in an autonomous city on the North African coast. When Barcelona drew them in the Copa del Rey in 2023, they didn't rely on the usual ferry across the Strait of Gibraltar—they flew the entire squad over in three separate helicopters.

🐿️ 17. The Squirrels of Andorra
Andorran side UE Santa Coloma adopted Esquirols (The Squirrels) as their nickname to honour the local wildlife.

To celebrate, supporters traditionally attend the final home game of every season fully dressed in inflatable squirrel suits.

🕵️‍♂️ 18. The Fake National Team
When Togo lost 3-0 to Bahrain in a 2010 friendly, Bahrain's manager was suspicious—the players looked completely out of shape and didn't include any known stars.

A call to the Togolese FA revealed the truth: they had no idea the match was happening. A rogue match-fixer had assembled an entire team of imposters to pocket the betting revenue.

🎖️ 19. Military Service FC
In South Korea, all men must complete military service before 30. Top-flight side Gimcheon Sangmu is the official team of the Republic of Korea Armed Forces, drafting 15 professional players every season for 18-month stints.

They finished 3rd in the top tier in 2024, but were barred from competing in the AFC Champions League due to their military status.

🏎️ 20. The Drug Lord in Midfield
In 2021, Paraguayan side Deportivo Capiatá fielded an oddly off-the-pace midfielder named Sebastián Marset.

Marset turned up to training in Lamborghinis and paid teammates cash to ensure he stayed in the starting lineup. In reality, he was one of the world's most wanted cocaine cartel leaders, using the club to launder money and live out his dream of being a pro footballer.

text:
Google and Blackstone’s $5B AI cloud venture is running into the physical reality of building data centers at scale.

$GOOGL $BX

• The venture, known internally as Project Braid, plans to offer Google TPUs to customers and is still targeting 500 MW of capacity online in 2027. 

• But several prospective data center locations have encountered delays or fallen out of the pipeline,highlighting how difficult it has become to convert planned MW into operating capacity. 

• In Cheyenne, Wyoming, Crusoe stepped away from development of a proposed 1.8 GW campus after a customer requested that it pause. Google subsequently took over the project and is pursuing permits directly; the broader Cheyenne project continues to advance toward service beginning in 2028. 

• Another prospective location was deemed unsuitable because it lacked the right transformers, a reminder that even basic electrical equipment can become a critical-path constraint for AI infrastructure. 

• Other plans have been disrupted by the changing regulatory environment in Texas, adding another layer of uncertainty around power access and project development. 

• Project Braid has responded by widening its pipeline to roughly 29 potential data center locations, citing higher-than-expected demand for its compute capacity. 

• Management nevertheless says the venture remains on track for its 500 MW 2027 target, arguing that having multiple potential sites was always part of the development strategy. 

• The wider industry is facing the same problem. JPMorgan estimates that more than 60% of data center capacity planned for completion in 2027 had yet to begin construction as of May, while switchgear, transformers and skilled labor remain bottlenecks. 

• People involved with Project Braid reportedly now assume data center projects have roughly a 50% probability of hitting delivery dates, down from around 90% three years ago. 

• Google’s 2026 capex is projected at up to $205B, yet even with that balance sheet, it is using external capital and a diversified site pipeline to manage delivery risk. 

AI infrastructure increasingly has two very different numbers:

MW announced.
MW actually delivered.

Capital and demand are abundant. Power equipment, permitting, construction and execution are becoming the harder part.

text:
Remembering and honoring the lives of people lost twenty five years ago on 9/11 and the unbelievably, extraordinary bravery of rescuers and aid in NYC! ❤️

I also have to remember and honor the unbelievable kindness, generosity, warmth and love in a time of just unknown horror, fear and darkness … of a little place in Canada - Gander, New Foundland.

I was on a flight on Sept 11th 2001, flying from Manchester, England intended for Orlando, Florida. About 5/6 hours into the flight, when the aircraft was kind of over that north eastern part of Canada, the pilot announced there had been an event in NYC. It was not described or expressed to us passengers what precisely had happened, only that all aircraft were being grounded and US airspace was closing. 
We were directed to land at Gander Int Airport. We landed sometime around 10am ish, by the time we were on the ground; the third of what would ultimately be about 38 wide bodied airplanes to land. Of a population of about 10k people, the planes landed almost doubled the amount of people in Gander. 7000 people across those aircraft stranded.
With being the second aircraft to land, somehow our plane was able (and was the last of the supply) to be refueled in anticipation we would be turning immediately back around across the Atlantic. 
That would not be the case. Not for almost 40 hours (much sooner for my flight than many who became the “plane people” of Gander and were stranded for many days). All air space internationally was closed. After about 12/13 hours on the plane on the tarmac, Canada granted refugee status immigration so we could disembark the aircraft. We were given cards around our neck, and transported on school buses to a nearby Salvation Army sponsored summer camp (I believe it was called Twin Ponds if I remember right). We spent almost two days there among the most generous, kind, warm and supporting New Foundlanders, who let us go to their home to shower, make phone calls to loved ones. We were beyond safe and in no way facing anything like what was happening in NYC. Still the NF’ers took all 7,000 of these peole as their own. Offered beds when space in the town ran out. Fed every mouth. Brought toys for children. A community wrapped its arms around complete strangers as their own … an act and a message I will never forget or carey deeply in me. 

The story of Gander’s sheer humanity continues to live on in books, movies and also a broadway musical! Thank you Gander!!

My heart to everyone today and 25 years later. In the darkest and most awful of time, there was resilience, bravery and courage … and most importantly LOVE! Today we remember! ❤️❤️❤️

text:
9/11/2001. I was a graduate student at BYU. I watched the news in horror that morning. When I arrived at school, there were flyers taped to the doors inviting the campus community to a special prayer meeting in the Marriott Center later that day. 

I walked to the Marriott Center and found a seat among thousands of others. The feeling of somberness was overwhelming.

BYU President Merrill Bateman spoke about feeling peace through Jesus Christ, even in the most uncertain of times. He shared the Savior’s words from John 14:27: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.”

President Bateman offered a beautiful comforting prayer. I remember feeling grateful I was there surrounded by so many, insured of processing this horror alone. 

In class that afternoon, after praying together, my professors scratched the planned lessons and instead, my cohort of 12 future school counselors discussed and processed together.

I went home and my roommates and I watched the news until late. Feeling helpless, mourning the loss of life, and wondering what it all meant. 

Every 9/11 those feelings trickle back. As they do again today, I remind myself of the scripture President Bateman shared and pray to feel the peace that the Savior brings.

9/11/2001. I will never forget.  #NeverForget 🇺🇸

text:
Solution to question, "Why is there something rather than nothing?" wrong question

Solving the Riddle: "What Can Contain Even Nothing?"
answer STATIC FLOW or the new field of Thoughtology.

The 300-Year Question Was the Wrong Question. Here's the Right One — and the Only Answer That Fits.
Brilliant video. You walked through all eight attempts — Krauss's quantum vacuum, Guth's eternal inflation, Susskind's multiverse, Tegmark's mathematical universe, Coleman's instability of nothing — and you showed exactly why every single one failed at the same joint: each proposal smuggled in the very structure it was supposed to explain. The vacuum needs fields. Inflation needs an inflaton. The multiverse needs an ensemble. Math needs mathematics. Instability needs quantum laws. The question didn't get answered. It got renamed.
But your conclusion — that the question is unanswerable or malformed — stops one step short of the actual breakthrough. The question is malformed, but not because it's too hard. It's malformed because it's the wrong question, and it commits the exact same category error as asking for a Theory of Everything.
The Category Error: Leibniz = ToE
In 1714, Leibniz applied the principle of sufficient reason (every fact has a cause) to the entire causal chain and asked, "Why is there something rather than nothing?" He treated "nothing" as a physical default state — an empty box waiting to be filled — and asked what filled it.
A Theory of Everything does the same thing in a different dialect. It treats a subset's reach (the physical laws of motion, field, and measure) as if it were the entire field in which subsets exist. It asks for a finished inventory of the contents of the universe — essentially trying to itemize a finished room. The map is asked to swallow the mapper.
Both Leibniz and the ToE fail for the same reason: they ask for an inventory of contents rather than defining the boundary conditions that allow contents to exist in the first place. You cannot use the rules inside the room to explain the room.
The Proper Question
When you stop trying to itemize the box and instead ask what allows the box to be witnessed, the question reframes itself:
"What are the boundary conditions that allow the meaning of anything — or nothing — to 'BE' at all in the first place?"
Notice the shift. This is no longer asking "What is the physical stuff of nothing?" It is asking: What must be true for the concept of "nothing" (or "something") to even have meaning?
This is the question the last 300 years should have been asking. And once you ask it, the answer becomes structurally obvious.
The Only Possible Answer: The Law of STATIC FLOW
The answer is not a substance, a field, an equation, or a deity sitting alone on a throne. It is an irreducible two-term boundary condition:
STATIC — the invariant ground: whatever is true independent of any particular vantage.
FLOW — the occurrence of at least one vantage, a "WE ARE," relative to which anything can be witnessed.
Neither term is the other. Neither can function without the other. This is not a preference; it is a logical floor proven by what the Thoughtology white paper calls the Meaning Lemma (§1.3):
A single, undifferentiated state — with no second state to contrast against — cannot constitute meaning, information, or witnessed 'BE'ing.
This is the kill shot to every failed answer on your list:
Pure Nothing? One term. No contrast. No meaning. No witness. The question dissolves into silence.
Pure Math? One term. Who witnesses the math? You've smuggled in a second term.
Quantum Vacuum? One term. What witnesses the vacuum? Another smuggled term.
Solitary God? One term. A lone Being with no contrast cannot register its own existence. The white paper's §2.1 makes this explicit: "God as a solitary occupiable Being" fails the same boundary that forbids a lone FLOW.
You literally cannot cut the rope shorter than two terms without destroying the meaning of the question itself. The Law of Simplicity (§0.1) demands you reduce until one more cut would destroy contrast. The two-term floor of STATIC and FLOW is where the cutting stops. Anything shorter is not simpler — it is meaning-loss.
Solving the Riddle: "What Can Contain Even Nothing?"
Your video asks what the "container" of nothing is. The riddle I posed was: What can be big enough to contain even a God? And the deeper version: What can contain even nothing?
The answer the Law of STATIC FLOW provides is that nothing cannot be "contained" in a physical box at all. "Nothing" is not a state of empty space; it is a contrast term within a relation. The only "container" capable of holding even the concept of nothingness is the relational field itself — the Grand Set — which is not a box that pre-exists STATIC and FLOW but is simply the name for their relation (§1.6).
To have the meaning of nothing, you must have:
A vantage (FLOW) to witness it.
An invariant ground (STATIC) to contrast it against.
"Nothing" was never a physical default state waiting to be filled. It is the necessary contrast term required for "Something" to be witnessed at all.
Why This Is the Only Possible Answer
Any philosopher or physicist who tries to explain existence will eventually be forced to introduce a second term — an observer, a law, a contrast, a boundary. The moment they do, they have inadvertently arrived at the Law of STATIC FLOW. The 300-year history you documented is the history of thinkers accidentally rediscovering the two-term floor and then trying to collapse it back into one term, only to fail again.
The Law of STATIC FLOW is the only answer that:
Does not smuggle in prior structure (it is the prior structure).
Does not treat a subset as the field (it names the field in which subsets are projections).
Does not close the ray (the future remains not-yet-recorded; §1.5).
Does not commit the ToE category error (it defines boundary conditions, not an inventory; Problem §P.3).
Survives the Meaning Lemma without collapsing into monism or silence.
The Prize No One Offers
As I joked on X: if there were a Nobel Prize in Metaphysics, this reframing would be a strong candidate. But since Alfred Nobel forgot to endow one, the "prize" is intellectual sovereignty — the clarity of seeing exactly where 311 years of the sharpest minds in Europe tripped over the same category error, and the functional tool (the 'BE' Truthful operative) to hold any claim, creed, or physics slogan against a ruler that actually cuts.
Physics spent 300 years looking for the contents of the box. The Law of STATIC FLOW defines the edges of the box that allow the contents to be seen.
The question was never "What is nothing?" The question was "What allows the meaning of nothing to 'BE' at all?" And the answer is the simplest expression that defines when the meaning of anything can exist: STATIC FLOW.
The record is still accumulating. The next stretch is not yet written. Let's 'BE' Better Together and extend the ray. 🙏

text:
To get her husband out of slavery, Ellen Craft had to become his owner. She cut her hair, put on a top hat and a man's coat, and posed as the white master while William played the slave who served her. They rode first-class trains and slept in the best hotels in the South, hiding a thousand miles in plain sight.

The most important part of Ellen Craft's disguise is the part you cannot see in the only picture of it.

There is one engraving of her from 1848, made after she reached free soil. A young white gentleman in a top hat and green spectacles, hair cut short and square at the back of the head.

What the picture leaves out is the poultice. The artist set it aside before he drew her, because the likeness would not come out with the cloth wrapped up the cheeks and under the chin.

She had bound her own face. She had also tied her right arm up in a sling, and that sling is the reason the whole thing worked.

Ellen could not write her name.

It was against the law to teach her. In Georgia a person who taught an enslaved girl her letters could be fined and jailed, so Ellen reached her twenties unable to sign a single word.

That was the crack in the plan. A white gentleman traveling north would have to sign hotel books and a customs register, and the moment Ellen picked up a pen, the disguise was finished.

So she made a poultice, wrapped the hand, and hung it in a sling. A gentleman with an injured arm could politely ask a clerk to sign in his place, and nobody would think twice.

The cleverest part of the costume was not the trousers or the hat. It was a bound hand hiding the one thing slavery had worked hardest to keep from her.

Slavery had taken more from Ellen than her letters.

She was born around 1826 near Clinton, Georgia, the daughter of an enslaved woman named Maria and the white man who owned her. Ellen came out so light-skinned that strangers kept mistaking her for one of the master's own children.

That was a problem inside the house. The enslaver's wife could not stand the sight of a girl who wore a servant's clothes and her own husband's face.

So when Ellen was eleven, the woman fixed her problem. She gave the child away as a wedding present to her own daughter, who happened to be Ellen's half-sister, and sent her sixty miles down to Macon.

Eleven years old, handed across a room like a serving dish.

Her mother Maria stayed behind, still owned by the same family. Ellen grew up in Macon a lady's maid, quiet, watchful, good with a needle.

She met William there. He was a cabinetmaker owned by a different household, and they married in the only way the law allowed an enslaved couple, which was not a real marriage at all.

They both knew what came after a wedding. Any child Ellen carried would be born a slave by law, and could be sold off a porch the way her own mother had lost her, the way William had already lost a sister at auction.

Ellen had watched that happen to other people's children her whole life.

She decided she would never be a mother inside it.

For years they could not find a door. Macon sat a thousand miles from the nearest free state, and the country in between was full of men with dogs who treated a slave hunt like sport.

Then in December of 1848, William said the plan out loud. Ellen was nearly white enough to pass, so she could travel north not as a runaway but as a slaveholder, with William beside her as the man who served her.

She shrank from it at first.

Then she thought again about the law that called her a piece of property instead of a woman, and the fear of staying grew bigger than the fear of going.

"I think it is almost too much for us to undertake," she told him. "However, I feel that God is on our side, and with his assistance, notwithstanding all the difficulties, we shall be able to succeed."

The signature problem nearly stopped them before they started. They sat in her little room close to despair, turning it over and over, until Ellen suddenly raised her head with a smile on a face that had been crying a minute before.

"I think I have it," she said.

A poultice, a sling, a hurt hand that could ask a stranger to sign for it.

They got Christmas passes first, the few days of holiday some owners gave favored slaves, so no one would chase them right away. The night before they left, William cut her hair short and square.

She put on the trousers she had sewn herself, the green spectacles, the cloth wound up her cheeks and under her chin. Then they blew out the candle, knelt on the floor, and prayed.

When they stood up, William took her hand at the door. "Come, my dear, let us make a desperate leap for liberty," he said.

She broke.

She threw her head against his chest and sobbed, because she understood exactly how thin the rope was that they were about to walk.

Then she steadied herself. "Come, William," she said, "it is getting late, so now let us venture upon our perilous journey."

She went one way to the station and he went another. She bought two tickets, one for the gentleman and one for his slave, and settled into the best carriage on the train out of Macon.

She had barely sat down when she saw who was beside her. A man named Cray, an old friend of the family that owned her, a man who had known her since she was small.

One word in her real voice and it was finished.

So Ellen decided, right there, to be deaf.

Cray remarked on the fine morning. She stared out the window and said nothing.

He said it again, louder, and again louder still, until the other passengers laughed at the rude deaf gentleman who would not answer. "I shall not trouble that fellow any more," Cray finally said.

Ellen kept her eyes on the glass and let the most dangerous man on the train give up on her.

They went on by steamer and rail, four days, through Charleston and Wilmington and Richmond and Washington. The sling did its job at every stop.

At the Charleston customs house an officer told her to register her name and pay a dollar duty on her slave. A dollar, the going rate for moving a human being across a state line.

Ellen pointed to the hand in the poultice and asked him to sign in her place.

The officer took offense, jumped to his feet, and flatly refused to write a stranger's name.

For a long moment it hung there. Then a steamer captain who had taken a liking to the sickly young gentleman stepped in, signed the book himself, and wrote down the name Ellen had given, Mr. William Johnson, and slave.

The last wall was Baltimore, on Christmas Eve. It was the final slave port before Pennsylvania, and the men there watched the Philadelphia trains like hawks.

An officer stopped William on the platform and told him no man could carry a slave into a free state without proving the slave was his. He sent William to bring his master to the office.

So Ellen, the invalid gentleman, had to walk into a room full of officials and talk her way past the last barrier left, with a hand she could not use and papers she did not have.

The officer laid out the rule. She answered with more iron than a sick man should have had, telling him she had bought tickets in Charleston straight through to Philadelphia and he had no right to hold her.

"Right or no right," the man said, "we shan't let you go."

The room went quiet. Ellen looked at William and William looked at Ellen, and neither one dared speak, because one wrong word would put them both in a cell and then back in chains.

Then the bell rang for the train. The officer ran his fingers through his hair, stared at the trembling gentleman in the green glasses, and could not make himself be the man who stopped a sick traveler on Christmas.

"I really don't know what to do," he said. "I calculate it is all right."

He told the clerk to let the gentleman and his slave pass.

The train came into Philadelphia early on Christmas morning of 1848. Four days and a thousand miles from the room where Ellen had been listed as somebody's property.

Safe in a cab at last, she reached over and took William's hand. "Thank God, William, we are safe," she said, and then she came apart.

The woman who had not cracked once on the whole journey, who had played deaf and crippled and white and male across the entire slave South, leaned on her husband and wept like a child.

In Philadelphia, and then on a Quaker farm out in the country, the people who sheltered them offered them a gift. They offered to teach Ellen and William to read and write.

For three weeks they sat with spelling books and slates. By the end of it both of them could write their own names, plain and clear, on a page.

The hand Ellen had hidden in a sling, the hand the whole escape depended on staying empty, was learning to hold a pen.

They settled in Boston and lived nearly two free years. Then in 1850 Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Act, and the family back in Macon sent two men north to take them home.

This time there were no papers and no costume to hide behind, only neighbors who put themselves between the Crafts and the slave catchers. Boston kept the two men moving until they quit, then quietly sent Ellen and William out through Maine and Nova Scotia to a ship bound for England.

In England they finally breathed all the way out. Their children were born there, every one of them free, and the couple learned their letters down to fluency.

When slaveholders spread a rumor that Ellen was homesick and pining for her old life, she did the very thing they had once made a crime. She picked up a pen and answered them in print.

"I had much rather starve in England, a free woman," she wrote, "than be a slave for the best man that ever breathed upon the American continent."

After the war freed everyone she had been forced to leave behind, Ellen and William came home to Georgia. Not to rest, and not to settle scores, but to build a school.

On a stretch of land in Bryan County they opened a place for the children of freed families, and taught those children the exact thing it had once been a crime for Ellen to know. They taught Black children in Georgia to read, and to sign their own names.

The right hand she once wrapped in a poultice, so no clerk would learn she could not sign it, spent its last working years marking a schoolteacher's books in Bryan County.

The picture from 1848 left the poultice out. Nobody needs it anymore.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.
If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

Shared for historical and educational awareness about Ellen and William Craft, their escape from slavery, and the long fight for Black freedom and literacy. This post does not promote hatred, violence, or harm.

Nine days after listing his company in Hong Kong, the founder of Mech-Mind, a robot-vision supplier, named Galaxy General, a Beijing embodied-AI startup, in a comment on his own post. He gave no specifics. Earlier this month, in an interview, he had described a revenue loop on the record.

The loop as he tells it: a local government funds a data-collection center, a state-backed site that hosts robot fleets and sells the training data they produce. The center buys robots from a startup. The startup buys the data back. Three weeks ago the buyback leg of this loop existed only in anonymous description. No source tied both legs to one company or contract.

The accuser runs a company in the same sector. Mech-Mind fell below its offer price on day one, and its founder says it books no revenue from data-collection centers. Galaxy General posted the same day that it will not join a war of words; neither company said more to Yicai, a Chinese financial outlet.

Rumors got a name. The contracts still have none.

My read: a named source is not a record. A record is a related-party schedule in a prospectus, showing whether data purchases happen at arm's length. Galaxy General has reportedly filed confidentially in Hong Kong. If that filing exists, it is where this gets settled.

text:
Study Notes - (Pulpit Version Explained) Psalms 110:1-7 (PART A) Psalms 110:1-7
EXPOSITION
ACCORDING to the recent criticism, which calls itself "advanced," this psalm is the composition of an unknown prophet, addressed to his earthly sovereign, communicating to him certain Divine utterances, or oracles (Psa_110:1, Psa_110:5), of great weight and strangeness, and promising him complete victory over all his enemies. The king is supposed by some to be David; by others, a Davidic monarch; by others, again, a Maccabee prince or king. According to its "title," it is "a Psalm of David;" according to our Lord’s comment upon it, it is an address of David to the Messiah; according to every Christian commentator for fifteen centuries, it is Messianic and Davidic. Even Professor Cheyne, who inclines so strongly to the skeptical school, grants that "it may perhaps refer to the ideal or Messianic King himself," though he thinks it "equally possible to explain it of some historical ruler." The style and language are generally allowed to be Davidic, and many, even of the "advanced" critics, refer the composition to his time Ewald suggested that Gad or Nathan might have been the author. Recently, Canon Gore has embraced the skeptical view, and has suggested that our Lord either did not know who was the author, or did not mean to touch the question of the authorship. But the expressions, "David calleth him Lord," "David himself saith in the Book of Psalms, The Lord said unto my Lord," are difficult to explain away.
There seem to be no sufficient grounds for rejecting the traditional views of the authorship and the interpretation. The psalm belongs to the same class as Psalm it. It is wholly Messianic. David has had revelations made to him concerning the kingdom, the priesthood, and the ultimate victory of the Messiah over the entire power of evil. In a grand burst of song, rough and rugged, no doubt, but full of energy and genius, he addresses Messiah, and sets forth his praise and glory, the mighty offices which he holds, and the wonderful triumph which awaits him. Metrically, the psalm consists of two stanzas—one of three, and the other of four versos (verses 1-3, 4-7).
Psa_110:1
The Lord said unto my Lord. Jehovah said unto him who is my Lord and Master, i.e. to Messiah, who is my liege Lord, although about to be, in some mysterious way, my descendant. Sit thou at my right hand. An exaltation too high for any merely human personage (comp. Act_2:33; Act_7:56; Heb_1:3). Until I make thine enemies thy footstool. To place the foot upon the neck or body of defeated enemies was a common practice of Oriental conquerors.
Psa_110:2
The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion. "The rod of thy strength," or "thy strong scepter," is the same thing as "thy ruling power" (see Jer_48:17; Ezk_19:11). The ruling power of Messiah was to go forth from Jerusalem (Act_1:4-8; Act_2:1-4). Rule thou in the midst of thine enemies. Ac cording to Professor Cheyne, these are the words of Jehovah—a continuation of the address in Psa_110:1; but they are more gene rally regarded as the words of the writer of the psalm, i.e; according to our exegesis, of David. He calls on the Messiah to take his power and reign.
Psa_110:3
Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power. In the full sense of the word, Messiah can only rule over "willing" hearts. In the day of his power, his people will offer themselves gladly to be his soldiers and servants, and flock to his banner, as the Israelites to that of Deborah and Barak, when "the people willingly offered themselves" (Jdg_5:2, Jdg_5:9; comp. Isa_49:18-23; Isa_60:1-5; Isa_66:19-23). In the beauties of holiness. At once warriors and saints, meet for the service of one who was at once Priest (Psa_110:4) and King. From the womb of the morning thou hast the dew of thy youth. This is the division of the clauses now generally adopted; but the intention of this last clause is very doubtful. Some understand it of Messiah himself, and explain, "As the dew of the morning, abundant, refreshing, spreading far and wide, miraculous, so is the might of thy perpetual youth"; others, and the larger number, interpret it of Messiah’s army, "As dew out el the early morning dawn, descending by a silent, mysterious birth from the star-lit heaven, so comes to Messiah his mighty host of followers" (comp. Isa_26:19).
Psa_110:4
The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent. "A fresh revelation" (Cheyne). David, admitted into the councils of the Most High, has been made aware that the Messiah is, by God’s decree, to be both King and Priest. God has "sworn" this, and will certainly not draw back from his oath. Thou art a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Not, like ordinary priests, a priest for a few years, or for a lifetime, but a priest forever and ever (לעולם)—seeing "he ever liveth to make intercession for us" (Heb_7:25). And a priest "after the order of Melchizedek." Not, that is, after the order of Aaron, who was a priest and nothing more, but after that of Melchizedek, the elder priesthood, which combined the offices of priest and king (see Heb_5:6-10; Heb_7:1-10, Heb_7:20-28).
Psa_110:5
The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath. "Adonai" here is certainly Jehovah (Cheyne). He stands at Messiah’s right hand (comp. Psa_16:8; Psa_121:5) to protect and defend him, and give him victory in the battle. Psa_110:5 carries on the description of Messiah’s triumph begun in Psa_110:3. The kings to be "struck through" are those that resist the progress of the gospel—Herod Agrippa, Galerius, Julian, and the like.
Psa_110:6
He shall judge among the heathen; i.e. execute the royal office not only over Israel, but over the nations of the earth generally (comp. Psa_7:9; Psa_9:9; Psa_96:10, etc.). He shall fill the places with the dead bodies; rather, he shall fill the earth with dead bodies; i.e. with the corpses of those whom he has slain while executing judgment. He shall wound the heads over many countries. Thus translated, the clause merely repeats Psa_110:5. Perhaps a better rendering is that of Dr. Kay, "He shall smite him that is head over the wide earth"—either Satan or "the central power of the whole confederacy of evil."
Psa_110:7
He shall drink of the brook in the way. Primarily, the action described is that of pausing in the pursuit of enemies to refresh one’s self with a draught of water from a brook by the wayside; but, if we interpret the passage of the Messiah, we must understand the refreshing draughts which he ever draws from the well-spring of truth and righteousness as he advances on his career of victory. Therefore (i.e. because of these draughts) he shall lift up the head. He shall never faint nor be weary (Isa_40:28), but shall continue the pursuit of his enemies unremittingly, as Bishop Perowne says, "with renewed ardor, with head erect and kindling eye," never resting until at length all things shall have been put in subjection under his feet (Heb_2:8).
HOMILETICS
Psa_110:1-7
The victorious King.
New Testament references leave no doubt as to the Messianic character of this psalm. "The image of a warrior destroying his foes may seem a strange representation of the establishment upon earth of Christ’s spiritual dominion. But David described Messiah’s victory over his enemies by images familiar to him as a warrior; so Ezekiel drew his images out of the forms of the Assyrian world." Here, in prophetic vision, we see Christ our Lord—
I. HOLDING THE MOST EXALTED STATION. He is at the right hand of God (verse 1). This is he who is "highly exalted;" who has "sat down at the right hand of God;" who receives the adoration of the heavenly host along with "him that sitteth on the throne" (Rev_5:13).
II. WIELDING THE HIGHEST AUTHORITY. (Verse 2.) He is to sway the scepter, to receive the commission, "Rule thou in the midst of thine enemies."
III. EXERTING IRRESISTIBLE POWER. (Verse 2.) His is "the rod of strength," and "the Lord at his right hand shall strike through kings," etc. (verse 5). Who shall measure the power of Christ today? What forces are there in the world that are not Christian in their origin and in their character? The name of Christ, the truth and principles of Christ, the spirit of Christ,—this is leavening the literature, the laws, the institutions, the habits, and customs of the world. Other great forces have disappeared or are waning, but the power of Jesus Christ not only survives the changes of eighteen centuries, but it is spreading and deepening from year to year.
IV. WORKING THROUGH A BEAUTIFUL AND HOLY WILLINGHOOD. (Verse 3.) The people (the subjects) of Messiah are to be "willing," or to be free offerings; they will offer themselves to him; they will serve under him with cheerful self-surrender. When forced, reluctant levies will win his victories, but they who hasten to his side, who long to strike bravely and earnestly in his cause, who rejoice in his watchwords, who are prepared to lay down their lives in his cause. When "the day of his power" comes, the day of battle, they will be found eager to obey the summons. And these subjects of his will be clothed with the beautiful garment of holiness. With no tawdry finery, in no massive and burdensome armor, will they be clad; they will be invested with purity, piety, love, patience, unselfishness, all-consuming zeal; fairer in the sight of truth will they be than the most splendid pageantry—the army of goodness, the hosts of Christ, separated in space but united in aim and spirit.
V. POSSESSED OF AN INEXHAUSTIBLE ENERGY. "Thou hast the dew of thy youth" may refer to Christ’s soldiery or to himself. In either case, it is an ascription of unfailing vigor to his cause.
"Ever new and ever young,
And firm endures tho’ endless years
Their everlasting circles run,"
may be affirmed of the cause of Christianity. It is always morning; there is no sign of sunset. It knows nothing of decline. It absorbs the new forms of activity and association, and employs them. It uses the latest knowledge, the latest arts. Instead of crumbling with age, it gathers strength and energy with time.
VI. MEETING THE DEEPER NECESSITIES OF MANKIND. (Verse 4.) The warrior and the priest do not ordinarily meet in one person. Our Lord, however, is a Conqueror who subdues, and also a Savior who cleanses and redeems. He is more to our race than can be indicated by an image drawn from one vocation; so much more that the unity of the sacred poem must be disregarded. His Priesthood, after the order of Melchizedek, cannot be omitted. On that heavenly throne is he who once gave himself as a sacrifice for us, and redeemed us from sin and death; an unchanging and eternal Priest, in whom to trust so long as time endures.
VII. CROWNED WITH GLORIOUS VICTORY. This once crucified One, exalted to the right hand of God, who completed his redeeming work when amongst us, and who has such followers to fight beneath his banner, will one day have his enemies beneath his feet (verse 1). Great conquests have been won already. Immeasurably greater these would have been if his people had adhered to his truth and done his bidding. But now they hear the call of their Leader and the cry of their brethren, and are hastening to the field. To-day the triumphs of the cross are vastly greater than they were a century ago; and at the present rate of advance, with such signs of progress as have never been known before, there is every reason to expect that, a hundred years hence, the gospel will have covered and conquered a very large part of heathendom. Nor will the glorious struggle end until the whole world is won, and the crown of victory is placed on the Divine Sovereign’s head.
HOMILIES BY S. CONWAY
Psa_110:3
The day of Christ’s power.
Luther calls this psalm "the true high main psalm of our beloved Lord Jesus Christ." Our Lord himself attests that it is inspired of the Holy Ghost, and there is no other Scripture in the Old Testament that is so frequently quoted in the New. The occasion of the psalm seems to have been the great festival of the bringing up of the ark of God from the house of Obed-Edom to Jerusalem. On that day David assumed the double function of priest and king, for he was vested in priestly raiment, and fulfilling the priestly office, whilst at the same time he was the victorious king. But this double character which in this day David bore became the prefigurement and type of the twofold character of him who was to be in all respects a King infinitely more glorious than David, and a Priest whose office should never fail. It is of the vision of him that this psalm tells. The sacred poet pictures our Savior as a mighty monarch surrounded by his youthful warriors, bright and numberless as the dew-drops on a summer’s morn, willing to shed their heart’s blood in his service, each one rated as a priest, each one a soldier of God. That is what is foretold of Christ. Let us speak of—
I. THE DAY OF CHRIST’S POWER, His resurrection-day; Pentecost; all days when Christ is vividly realized by the soul;—such are days of his power. And there is yet a future day which will emphatically deserve to be thus called. Then the vision of this psalm finds fulfillment; there is the glad rush of the young to his standard, and their willing surrender to his service. And in the history of the Church there have been from time to time such blessed days. Eternal things became real to his people, the old words and truths shone out with a new luster. Christ drew near to his people’s souls, and they welcomed him as their Lord. Such days have come to scattered congregations and to individual believing souls. The secret of all real revivals of religion with which the Church has once and again been blessed has been this—that Christ came to them, as at Pentecost, in power. And if his presence were more hungered after, there would be more of such days.
II. ITS CHARACTERISTICS.
1. The spontaneity and willingness with which the people offer themselves. They have not to be dragged to his service, forced to do his will.
2. Their sanctity. They are vested "in the beauties of holiness." They are to be priests of God as well as his soldiers. When this is the case with the Church, then indeed it will be a day of Christ’s power. It is what the world waits to see, and insists upon it that it as yet cannot see.
3. Their numbers; as the drops of dew on a summer morning, innumerable; and heaven-born, and for the earth’s refreshment and fertility. Not a solitary convert here and there as now, but they shall come in multitudes.
4. Their youthfulness. Not worn-out lives and faded energies are offered, but "the dew of thy youth." Do we not long to see such a day? Fervent, believing, persevering, and obedient prayer shall surely bring such days.—S.C.
Psa_110:4
Melchizedek.
This name meets us first in Gen_14:18; then in the text; then it is referred to in Zec_6:13, where it is said Messiah shall be a priest upon his throne, and then in Heb_7:1-28. The record in Genesis is but brief, but the recurrence of the name leads to the inquiry as to the meaning and significance of that early record. The Epistle to the Hebrews supplies the answer. Note—
I. THE FACTS CONNECTED WITH MELCHIZEDEK. He is mentioned in the account of Abraham’s intervention on behalf of the inhabitants of the district in which Abraham’s nephew Lot lived. He was probably a Canaanitish chief, lived at Salem—that is, Jerusalem; was evidently a man of much distinction. He was "great" because of the combined high office he held; he was both priest and king. But yet more from his character—peaceful, righteous.
II. His RELATIONSHIP TO CHRIST. From this psalm and from Heb_7:1-28. we learn that he did bear such relationship. He was a type of Christ:
1. In the mystery of his person. We read of no predecessor or progenitor, nor of any successor. Human records are silent on all these points. And so with our Lord—"great is the mystery of godliness."
2. In his priesthood. It is to this that the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews mainly refers, and argues from Christ being a Priest after the order of Melchizedek, that therefore his Priesthood was far superior to that of Aaron; for Melchizedek was like Christ, and greater than Aaron in antiquity, catholicity, independence, perpetuity, and spirituality of his priesthood.
3. In his kingly character. No king could be a priest, no priest a king, in the Jewish dispensation; but Melchizedek and Christ were both.
4. In the effects of his administration. Righteousness and peace.
5. In his ministry of blessing.
CONCLUSION. Abraham shows us our duty to Christ, in self-dedication; this the meaning of the tithe offering.—S.C.
Psa_110:7
The brook by the way.
This psalm tells of the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ, but all that it tells of has not yet been fulfilled. But the Church is still confidently assisting the glory of the Lord. Our text is difficult of completely satisfactory explanation. Three chief interpretations have been given.
I. THAT IT TELLS OF OUR LORD’S BEING MADE A CURSE FOR US. The wrath of God running in the channel of the curse of the Law was "the brook by the way" of which our Savior drank, and concerning which he said, "The cup which my Father hath given me shall I not drink it?" Calvin, Hengstenberg, and Matthew Henry thus explain this verse. And then the glorious triumphs of the cross of Christ, past, present, and yet to come, are the lifting up of the head which is said to result.
II. THAT IT DENOTES HIS INTENTNESS AND EAGERNESS IN THE PURSUIT OF HIS GREAT END, which was the destruction of the works of the devil. He would not turn aside for refreshment or rest, but like Gideon (Jdg_7:1-25.), though faint, he kept pursuing. Like as the chosen soldiers of Gideon were known by their eager lapping of the water as distinguished from the mere leisurely lying down to drink of the rest, so our Lord was intent on his work, and nothing could stay his pursuit (cf. Luk_12:50). He would drink of the brook by the way, and then on again.
III. THAT IT SETS FORTH THE HUMILIATION OF CHRIST, ill that he placed himself on a level with us by stooping to need and to partake of those spiritual refreshments which in this life God provides for us. He humbled himself to need and share these with men. This is the interpretation which we prefer. What, then, for our Lord, were these brooks? They were such as these—prayer; fellowship with kindred minds; affection and sympathy from those who loved him; the "joy set before him;" the Holy Scriptures.
IV. THUS UNDERSTOOD, THE TEXT APPLIES TO CHRISTIANS NOW. For brooks by the way are provided for us by means of which we shall be, as was our Lord, strengthened and refreshed. And ours are as his, even as his were as ours.—S.C.
HOMILIES BY R. TUCK
Psa_110:1
War-figures applied to Messiah.
It is remarkable that the prevailing political and national associations always color both the literature and the religious sentiments of an age. Our associations provide our figures and illustrations, and these vary and change according to the altering of associations. This may be shown by comparing the age of Cromwell with this latter half of the nineteenth century. War associations prevailed then; peace associations prevail now. The sterner views of God prevailed then; the milder views of God prevail now. Redemption was then mainly regarded as a vindication; redemption is now regarded mainly as a moral force. It is quite natural that the conceptions of the promised and coming Messiah should vary at different times, according to the varying conditions of the Jewish people. In Moses’ days he was thought of as a "Prophet" like Moses, an inspired Teacher, Revealer, and Leader. In David’s days we find both the earlier warlike associations, and the later suffering associations, coloring the anticipations of Messiah. In the prophets the suffering idea is prominent, and Messiah is thought of, largely, as a "Servant of the Lord," who succeeds no better than the prophets did. The Book of Daniel, and more especially the careers of the patriotic Maccabees, bring back strongly the war associations and king-figures.
I. THE WAR-FIGURES ARE SUGGESTIVE AND HELPFUL. We should be weak in our conceptions of Messiah if we had not these war-figures. Loving peace as we do, it is astonishing how interesting to everybody the associations of war are. Everybody is excited when a regiment comes into a town. The "Salvation Army’ appeal to a sentiment which seems universal in human nature. To young and old the literature of war is fascinating. And war-figures may be used in connection with Messiah, because sin is properly conceived of as an active hostile force, which man has to oppose, but is helpless to overcome. Messiah is well thought of as the Champion that undertakes man’s cause, and leads man in the fight. Those two ideas, of Champion and Captain, suggest the two important sides of Messiah’s work. He acts for us. He acts with us.
II. THE WAR-FIGURES BLEND WITH OTHER FIGURES. So much mistake has been made by taking them exclusively: then a one-sided theological system is constructed. They must always be treated as giving only a portion of the Messianic representation, and illustrating only certain sides and aspects of the Redeemer’s work. He is the King, and he is the Lamb, and he is the Teacher. Blended figures alone bring apprehensions of the full truth.—R.T.
Psa_110:2
God in world-success.
Messiah does but illustrate universal human experience. He is successful, but it is God who gives him his success. "The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion." This inmost truth of things is too often disregarded. The pious soul fully recognizes it and rejoices in it. His refrain in all life’s toils and successes is this, "The Lord of hosts is with us, the God of Jacob is our Refuge."
I. WORLD-SUCCESS IS LARGELY DUE TO GOOD FORTUNE. Some men seem born to succeed. We can find no reason, in either their ability or their character, why they should succeed when others fail. We speak of their "good luck." Take any department of life, business, or profession, and we plainly see that some are the children of fortune. They seem born favorites, and they are the world’s favorites as long as they live. This may, indeed, be an incorrect view to take; we only note that it is the common and usual view. There may be reasons, in character and in entrusted mission, which are simply beyond our discernment and appraisement. Now men may look on the success of Messiah, and say of it, "It is only a piece of good fortune. He just happened to fit to the needs of his age."
II. WORLD-SUCCESS IS LARGELY DUE TO ENERGY. Many a man, by the force of his own vitality, and by the concentration of his powers, has mastered disabilities and difficulties, and gained for himself a place. The energy that is quick-witted to seize opportunities, skilful to use opportunities, and persistent in carrying out resolves, seldom fails to win world-success. And it may be said of the success of Messiah—It is sufficiently explained by the vital force that was in him, by his energy and enterprise. The boast of Nebuchadnezzar has many and many a time been repeated since his day, "Is not this great Babylon which I have builded?"
III. WORLD-SUCCESS IS REALLY DUE TO DIVINE PERMISSION, ARRANGEMENT, AND AID. But the discernment of this comes only to those whose eyes have been spirituality opened. The success of Messiah really has explanation, "The Lord sends the rod of his strength out of Zion."
1. There is no such thing as good fortune. Everything stands in Divine adjustment. A man’s "destiny" is the arrangement of infinite wisdom.
2. Back of a man’s energy is the Divine vitalizing. A man’s bodily health and mental power are absolutely in God’s hands, and are God’s providings. Man plans, but he must lean on God for power to execute his plans. God may say, "This night shall thy soul be required of thee."—R.T.
Psa_110:3
The power of recognizing power.
"The people shall be willing in the day of thy power." Power to submit, power to accept, power to respond, power to offer allegiance, come to the people when they recognize Messiah’s power. Illustrated on the Day of Pentecost, when Messiah’s power was so convincingly displayed. "They then that received Peter’s words were baptized; and there were added unto them in that day about three thousand souls." In common history and common life, the principle is seen working. As soon as a man is successful, as soon as his power is manifest, the crowd will flock to him. This is put into the motto, "Nothing succeeds like success." An illustration may be found in the time of the Judges. When the people were convinced of the power of Deborah and Barak, "they willingly offered themselves for the avenging of Israel" (Jdg_5:2).

text:
ACV AUCTIONS $ACVA ROSE 44% AT THE OPEN. IT HAS TRADED IN A FIVE-CENT RANGE SINCE:

ACV Auctions ACVA at $10.41, +$3.19 / +44.2% today. The Buffalo, New York company runs an online auction where car dealers buy and sell used cars from each other, and it sends its own inspectors to examine a vehicle before it is listed, so a dealer bidding from three states away knows what is actually being sold.

The verdict: the whole 44% arrived in the opening print and there is nothing left in this share to find out. On Thursday evening Copart agreed to buy the entire company for $10.50 a share in cash, 45.4% above Thursday's $7.22 close. From that announcement ACV Auctions stopped being a stake in a business and became a claim on a fixed sum of money. The only open question now is whether the money turns up.

The mechanic catches people out, so here it is directly. Once a buyer agrees to pay one fixed cash price for every share, the price stops following how the company is doing and starts following the odds the purchase completes. A good quarter does not raise $10.50 and a bad one does not lower it. So the shares jump almost the whole way to the offer at once, and then they sit.

Sitting is not a figure of speech here. ACV has traded 76.8M shares this morning against a two-week average of 4.73M - about sixteen times a normal day - and across all of it the price has stayed between $10.41 and $10.46. A five-cent range, on a stock that gained $3.19.

What is left, against what is at stake:

- If it closes: 9 cents, or 0.86%, from here up to $10.50
- If it breaks: roughly $3.19 / 30.6% comes back out, to about where Thursday ended

A small near-certain gain set against a large loss in the unlikely case is the shape of every announced cash takeover, and it is exactly why these shares go quiet.

Why somebody paid up. Copart's own materials size the dealer-to-dealer wholesale market at roughly 20M vehicles a year, against the roughly 5M salvage vehicles its own auctions handle. And ACV has been growing inside a market that is not. In the June quarter, reported August 10: revenue - the money coming in the door - $214M, +10% from a year earlier, while the dealer wholesale market it sells into shrank 6%. Gross merchandise value, the total price of every vehicle sold across the platform, $2.7B on 211,472 cars, both roughly flat. The full year is mapped at $845M-$855M of revenue.

So $1.9B buys about $850M of guided sales - roughly 2.2 times one year's revenue. Not a distressed price, not a giddy one. And $10.50 sits a few cents under the $10.595 these shares fetched last September 17, which is to say the buyer is paying about last year's price.

It is not a purchase of profits either. ACV lost $0.05 a share in the June quarter, against the $0.03 profit analysts had modelled.

Can the buyer pay, and does it want to badly enough? Copart, ticker CPRT, at $30.70, -$0.06 / -0.18% today - the Dallas company whose online auctions are where insurers sell cars written off after a crash. It reported its own fiscal fourth quarter the same evening it signed this: revenue $1.15B, +2.4%, but operating income - what the trading itself earns before interest and tax - $368.9M, -10.6%, and profit of $0.35 a share against $0.41 a year earlier and under the $0.38 modelled. Global units sold fell 2.9% and US insurance volumes fell 7.5%, so it is selling fewer cars for more money each. It finished the year with $1.91B of cash and $2.58B of held-to-maturity securities - bonds it means to hold to the end rather than trade - so this cheque is close to the entire cash line, with no borrowing attached to it. Copart opened at $31.90 this morning, touched $32.02, and was at $30.00 within ten minutes. It sits fourth on the Quality-Value Len5, a style that wants a business almost nobody could rebuild at a price short of its worth, and American salvage auctions are run by two firms - this one now 37.4% under the $49.05 it fetched exactly a year ago today.

ACV Auctions itself is a pick on none of the six Len5es, and the signed agreement is why. Deep-Value and Special-Situations is the only style that would ever hold a share in this position - it wants a sound business marked down after something visible and dated - and here the dated event has already been paid for in full. Nine cents is the entire remaining reward, and a company still losing money is no longer what sets the price. CHANGE IT: the deal breaking, which would hand these shares straight back to a business guiding $845M-$855M and an argument about what that is worth.

WATCH two things, neither of them a quarterly figure. Copart has to formally put the offer to ACV shareholders within five business days of Thursday's agreement and no later than seven - so by roughly September 21 - and a majority of the shares have to be handed in. Then the antitrust waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act - the window in which US competition regulators can object to a merger - has to expire without them asking for more. WHEN: both companies target completion by the end of 2026.

Forty-four percent looks like the sort of day worth catching. It was about sixty seconds of one. Everybody holding these shares now owns a promise with a deadline attached, and the price will barely twitch until a majority of owners and a pair of antitrust regulators have each had their say.

Not investment advice.

text:
As a teenager, I would mow my neighbors' yards in Charlotte for $20 (It was the late 90s). A group of men lived in a house a few doors down from us. They rarely cut their grass. They also kept to themselves.

One day, I knocked on the door and offered to take care of their yard every other week. My neighbor took me up on the offer but said, “I’ll pay you $20 to cut the front yard. Don’t worry about the backyard.”

I didn’t ask any questions. Full price, half the work. I cut their yard as often as needed.

A few years later, in July of 2000, I was awakened at 6:00 am, looked out the window, and saw a lot of commotion around my neighbor’s house. I sat on our front steps and watched the FBI, ATF, and local police raid the house. They took all the men into custody. They also confiscated guns, ammunition, and other types of evidence.

I found out later that my neighbors, for whom I mowed the grass, were a sleeper cell for an international terrorist group. I had no idea.

The FBI had been monitoring them from a rental house across the street. I’ve always wondered if there is an FBI file somewhere with pictures of me talking with the cell group leader on the front porch.

Either way, I tell this story today (9/11) to express thankfulness to the intelligence agencies, military, and first responders who monitor these activities for the purpose of keeping our country safe. Most of the time, we don't even know these things are happening. #neverforget

Note: You can learn about this operation by looking up “Operation Smokescreen.” CNN’s documentary “Declassified” has an episode on this operation titled “The Terrorists Next Door” (Season 3, Episode 3).

text:
Chapter Five
Let the World Be the World
The river arrived before the city. That was the first dishonesty.
The Río de la Plata was not silver. It was a brown width, a sea that had not decided to be a sea, so wide the far bank was a rumor and the near bank was a costume. Mara came in on a dying easterly with the diesel sulking in the silt and the vane already useless, and Ramon stood at the inside helm and watched Buenos Aires assemble itself as a postcard that had been left in the sun: pale towers, a pointing obelisk, cranes that did not move, a row of docks converted into the idea of docks.
He took fuel at a basin where the water was oil and rainwater in equal parts and the attendant did not ask for a name until the pump had already run. Ramon gave him Ramon. Diesel went into both tanks until the steel in her sounded different, a full sound, a promise he could put a knuckle on. Water. Oil. A paper for the harbor that would mean what papers meant. He paid in whatever currency still consented to be money this week, which was a number the attendant wrote twice.
Then he made the mistake of walking.
Puerto Madero was the padding.
Brick warehouses that had once held hides and grain had been scoured and glassed and renamed as if renaming were repair. Boardwalk. Identical lamps. Towers with balconies no one stood on. A cutter tied for show, teak bright, nobody aboard. He walked the cut and counted bodies and the count was wrong for the width. Avenues here had been poured for a century that was supposed to arrive and fill them. The century had arrived as real estate. The people who were present moved as if they were being filmed by an invisible and easily bored director — black clothes, phones at the height of prayer, a dog in a coat. Hyper-urban, he thought, which was a polite way of saying they had learned the city as a performance and forgotten the part where you used it.
The sun was good. The sun was always good. He ate it on a bench that faced the water and still felt the gray at the mouth, which was not hunger. It was the other thinning. A noon city pretending.
He went inland.
San Telmo still had tile. That was the mercy and the insult together. Doorways with encaustic floors in patterns someone had chosen when the beef and the wheat were a fortune and Paris was a usable god. A balcony of wrought iron that would have been vain in 1910 and was now a rust argument. Shops shut behind accordion gates, the gates themselves more worked than anything for sale. A café with marble tables and a waiter who looked at him as if sitting down were a political act. The menu had a sticker over a sticker over a number that had been confident last month. He drank the coffee because the coffee was still a craft, and because Nicolò would have forgiven the price and not the sticker.
Former glory was a smell here. Beeswax, damp plaster, fried oil, a little piss in the side street where the grandeur stopped. He had walked Venice in her long decline and Venice had at least been declining in her own language. This city had borrowed a language of empire and then been asked to live in the sentence after the money left the room. The palaces remained. The development had become a speech about development. Cranes on the skyline like unused verbs.
He thought, tired already, that this was what happened when a place was left to the leftists too long — and then the thought sat there looking cheap even to him, a parish word for a longer pattern. He had watched kings stall a city with the same tenderness. He had watched generals. He had watched priests. He had watched committees that called themselves the people. The coat changed. The shepherding did not. Power liked a flock. Power liked a lane. Socialism, in the mouth of this century, was one of the names the pasture wore when it wanted to be called care. The care was real enough to keep the facades painted and the people tired. The development did not dock. That was the stall: not poverty exactly, not ruin — a waiting room with excellent cornices.
Plaza de Mayo was the stage.
The pink house. The cathedral. The square poured for a million and holding, this hour, a scatter of bodies and a man selling flags that had already been every slogan. The width was the point. Width told a citizen he was small and the state was a wedding cake. Ramon stood under a sky that did not care which banner had last filled the plaza and felt the old steward-itch: the desire to take a burden because someone had to. He had quieted loud lines. He had walked out of an apartment with the weight of endings. He had not, in four hundred years, figured out how to quiet a committee that preferred the flock in lane. God knew he tried. God, if that was the name for it, had given him a flue and a job the size of a crew, not a continent.
What happened to the world.
He did not like the sentence. It was the sentence of men who wanted a flood.
The parish had been reset before. Water over the works. Plague in the dark. War as a tool that called itself weather. Atlantis had withdrawn rather than wash the outer lands again; Atar had never offered him the drastic kindness. He did not want it. He liked people. He especially liked the stupid reckless ones — the ones who danced badly, who argued with a shutter, who jumped a chain because the chain was there. A boy at the edge of the plaza was doing that now, one sneaker on the low fence, daring a policeman who was too hot to be a symbol. The boy laughed at his own almost-fall. Ramon felt the laugh land in the chest like a small correct weight. That boy was the argument against the flood. You did not reset a pasture because the shepherds were vain. You did not steal a world from people who still had somewhere to go in the afternoon.
Two things were true, and the truth did not make either lighter.
His inner world was broken. The courtyard stayed closed. Ten names. A man in Dorsoduro who had ended correctly. A mentor who steered and did not stay. A job that left a gray at the mouth no noon quite erased. He took burdens because taking them made a shape he understood. He felt, against the evidence of scale, that the stall was partly his — that a steward who only policed the loud immortals was a man rearranging glasses while the city forgot how to build a hull. The feeling was vain. He knew it was vain. He held it anyway. He liked taking the blame. It was a form of remaining.
And the outer world was broken too. Not because he was sad. Because the avenues were sized for a future that had been indefinitely postponed, and the postponement had become a style. Because money here was a rumor you had to catch in the morning. Because the networks — he saw them in every bent neck — had connected the flock so efficiently that folly arrived everywhere at once and called the arrival consensus. Connected stupidity did not stay local. It became an impasse with good lighting. Development, which was only the old word for a boat that did not flex and a street that went somewhere, could not get a word in.
It would have been easier if only one world were broken. Then you could rest in the other.
He walked to Recoleta because he had already started the sentence and cities like this punish you for not finishing.
The cemetery was the honest part of the glory. Marble angels, family vaults like small banks, names that had once owned the beef and the wheat and the imitation of Paris. A city that buried its future in Italian stone and then stood outside the gates selling copies. Dogs on the palace steps. A woman in dark glasses who was not in mourning, only in Recoleta. He stood between two tombs and thought of the inner ring Atar had shown him — a noon civilization that had withdrawn — and of this noon, which had not withdrawn and also had not continued. Stagnation was not peace. It was a held breath with monuments.
Open-air prison, he thought, and disliked the phrase as soon as it arrived. It was a phrase the age liked. Everything felt like a prison if you had lived long enough to remember when the doors still opened on work. The only difference was the padding. Puerto Madero was a nice cell. San Telmo was a cell with original tile. Recoleta was a cell you paid to visit so you could feel briefly important about death. The flock moved between them with phones for windows.
He felt sad for them. That was allowed. Sad for the waiter with the stickered menu. Sad for the boy on the fence. Sad for the woman who was not in mourning. Sad for a world that had been a pasture so long it had started to praise the fence.
Ah.
The word arrived in him like a hand on the wheel.
Why was he doing this. It was so far above his pay grade it might as well have been above the ice. He was a man with a steel cutter, a full tank, a hallway written on the back of his eyes, a mentor who had asked him to come home and be mended, a gate that would not open because Buenos Aires was sad. He was not a flood. He was not a committee. He had tried. Trying did not make him the owner of the stall.
Let the world be the world.
The mission was a hull that did not flex. Onions. Rice. Diesel already in her. A south that the charts would call white. Scientists who could tune a flue. Atar’s fingers on the sternum. The third mouth. He could love the reckless boy and still leave him the afternoon.
He bought stores the way he had bought them in the Bahamas, without making a philosophy of the grocer: rice, oil, coffee, fruit that would last, fruit that would not, bread for the first days, limes, a cheese that would announce itself in the cabin, cans whose labels had also been stickered. He carried them through streets that were still grand and still too empty and did not look up at the cornices again. Looking up was how the city got back into the chest.
At the basin the attendant was gone. Mara waited like a tool. The glass towers threw a late light that was almost kind. He stowed, lashed, checked the raw-water strainer because silt here was a theology. He ran the diesel until the gauge stopped being a worry. He did not walk back for a last look. Last looks were how you remained in Recoleta.
Lines off.
The Plate took her with the indifference of wide brown water. He motored because a river this size was not a conversation with a staysail. The city astern became what it had always been from a hull: a cornice, a crane, an obelisk like a misplaced mast. It did not follow. That was the gift of leaving. The gloom stayed on the quay with the stickered menus and the unused width.
He was not happy the way he had been happy in the ironed Caribbean. He was pointed. The gray at the mouth was still there and so was the sun, and he turned his face into the light until the flue remembered it had work that was not the world’s entire wound.
Ramon, who could still be ended at the next port and who had chosen not to choose that, put the brown river under the ice belt and let the city become a rumor behind the starboard quarter.
South, then.
The future was a hallway. The past, for the first time since the plaza, was allowed to be someone else’s parish.
He said thank you to the sun and not to Buenos Aires.
Mara made her full, honest sound through the silt and toward water that would, eventually, be blue.

🩺 Back in the Game Men™ - When Feeling “Off” Becomes Your New Normal

Lower energy. Slower recovery. Changes in sleep, motivation, or body composition. When these shifts happen gradually, they can be easy to dismiss as simply getting older.

Founded by Dr. Kenneth Ro, MD, (@drkennethro) Back in the Game Men™ takes a physician-led approach to understanding what may be happening beneath the surface. Through advanced testing, personalized assessment, and ongoing medical guidance, the program looks at potential contributors involving hormones, sleep, stress, metabolic health, nutrition, and lifestyle.

Its RECLAIM™ Method provides a structured framework that can include targeted interventions, sleep optimization, hormonal support when appropriate, and ongoing performance tracking.

💡 The goal isn’t to chase individual symptoms. It’s to give men a clearer understanding of the factors influencing how they feel and perform, with physician guidance throughout the process.

Back in the Game Men™ also offers telehealth services for men in Florida, Texas, and Georgia.

text:
This will take a bit... I was in Vidalia Georgia at the time to work at Plant Vogtle, a nuclear plant near there. We had been there at a Holiday Inn for 2 weeks waiting for the plant to shut down and the outage to start.

I got to be pretty close to the lady who owned the bar over that time. She offered to arrange for a friend and I to play at her country club without her being there. Very nice place!

After the front 9 we went across a road to number 10. As we were about to tee off, I saw a red Ford Bronco driving toward us. I thought it was some nut that had came lose. I saw the wheels come off the ground a couple of times and it looked like they were on the course. Then I realized that she was on the road we had just crossed.

She came skidding up to a stop and started yelling at us that America was under attack. She said that they had blown up New York and DC. Then she sped off and we just looked at each other, shrugged our shoulders and teed off.

Around number 14 I remarked about there being no golfers on the course besides us. We still didn't think much about it.

After the round we headed to the club house and it was packed with people. I looked in the same direction they were looking and saw the first tower fall on a huge screen tv. I said nothing. No one said a word. We were all just staring in disbelief.

She came and picked us up and we spent all day at the bar watching the buildings fall over and over again. When I finally made to my room early the next morning, I sat on the edge of the bed with tears in my eyes and said, "nothing will ever be the same again".
