text:
The Ministry of Fear: Why 57% of Defence Whistleblowers Hide Their Names

In the year 2024/25, 57% of defence whistleblowers chose to raise concerns anonymously, according to Cabinet Office transparency data.

There was a time when the military virtues were described rather simply: courage, discipline, obedience and loyalty. A soldier was expected to stand his ground, obey a lawful order and place the Corps, the regiment, the service and the country before himself.

What was discussed rather less often was what happened when loyalty required a man or woman to say that something inside the institution had gone wrong.

That is the uncomfortable territory entered by the Government’s newly published Whistleblowing in Defence Review, presented to Parliament on 9 September.

Its central finding is striking precisely because it is so ordinary. Confidence in speaking up depends not chiefly upon the existence of procedures, policies or telephone numbers, but upon culture, trust and leadership behaviour in practice.

In other words, the question is not simply whether a whistleblowing system exists. It is whether the person using it believes that the institution will protect the messenger as carefully as it protects the message.

The review makes 13 recommendations. 

It calls for clearer reporting routes, better understanding of the system, greater confidence in the independence of the confidential hotline and stronger reassurance that those who raise legitimate concerns will not find their careers or security clearances damaged as a consequence.

Yet there remains a curious distinction at the heart of the matter.

Members of the Armed Forces are not directly protected by the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 in the same way as civilian workers. The Ministry of Defence says comparable protections are extended through Defence policy, and the review concludes that the principal weakness lies not in the law but in the way the system operates.

That may be so.

But history has taught us that policy and power do not always sit comfortably together. 

Consider MI5 and HMG’s doctrine of “Neither Confirm Nor Deny” — NCND — a policy, not a law, which was used to shield the Security Service (“MI5”) from scrutiny even as false evidence was put before three separate courts during proceedings, concealing illegality and protecting the institution from public accountability.

The courts found that they had been misled. 

We already know that false evidence was knowingly given under oath. We have another, rather older word for that: perjury.

And yet the obvious question remains — has anyone gone to jail?

The answer, so far, is no.

A protection written into statute carries a very different weight from an assurance offered by a department whose own conduct may one day be called into question.

Which brings us back to that figure.

Fifty-seven per cent.

More than half of those who spoke up preferred not to attach their names to what they were saying.

For an institution built upon courage, that is a deeply troubling prospect for Whitehall and national security.

The old military tradition asked men and women to show courage in the face of the enemy. The modern State must also be prepared to recognise another kind of courage: the courage required to tell one’s own commanders, colleagues or department that something is wrong.

And that is where the Ministry of Defence now faces its real test.

It is not enough to publish a review, accept recommendations or point to a confidential telephone line. 

The MOD must demonstrate, through cases and conduct, that those who raise lawful concerns will not be isolated, discredited, professionally damaged or quietly marked as troublesome.

Whistleblower protection cannot be measured by what a department says about itself. It must be measured by what happens to the person who speaks.

Until serving personnel believe that uncomfortable truths can be raised openly, in their own names, without fear of retaliation or career damage, the problem will not have been solved.

The most important question for the Ministry of Defence is therefore not whether it has a whistleblowing policy.

It is why, in 2024/25, 57 per cent of its whistleblowers believed anonymity was the safer course.

Until the MOD can answer that convincingly, the figure itself remains an indictment.

text: From Midlothian's Mayor Pro Tem  Representative Harrison posted this morning that Midlothian City Council "voted unanimously to raise property taxes." A few facts he left out. The rate we adopted is $0.64 per $100 of value, down from $0.65 last year. We cut the tax rate. Of the $5,560,152 increase in total property tax revenue, $5,001,958 of it 90 percent is new value added to the tax roll this year new homes and new businesses that didn't exist on last year's roll. The remaining $558,194 reflects rising appraised values on existing property, and even that is weighted toward non-homesteaded and commercial property, not owner-occupied homes. Texas caps how much a homestead's taxable value can rise each year. Commercial property and rentals have no such cap, so when values climb, they carry more of that increase every time. And regardless, because we cut the rate, the average existing homeowner's actual city tax bill is going down $64.53, not up. A lower rate on a higher value still nets out to real savings. This budget also keeps our general fund reserves above 150 days of operating expenses, well past the city's own 90 day minimum. That's what keeps our credit strong and our borrowing costs low on every road and facility we finance. The rest of the growth in revenue goes toward keeping police, fire, and streets in pace with a city that's still adding rooftops every month. Midlothian also has one of the highest local homestead exemptions in this region at 20 percent. I pushed to get that adopted, phased it in over two budget cycles starting in 2023, and I'll keep defending it. That exemption comes off your home's value before the tax rate is ever applied. And 20 percent isn't our choice to raise further  it's a hard state cap under the Texas Tax Code. Representative Harrison sits in the Legislature that set that cap. If he actually wants to lower property taxes, he could file a bill next session to raise or remove it and let cities like Midlothian give homeowners real, lasting relief. That would take more than a Facebook post. Based on his record so far, I'd rather see it than expect it. He also says he wants to eliminate property taxes altogether. That's not a plan, it's a slogan. Property taxes fund cities, counties, and schools. Getting rid of them means replacing billions of dollars in revenue with something else, and in every serious version of that conversation at the Capitol, that something else has meant a large increase in the state sales tax. Representative Harrison has never said what he'd replace that money with, what it would mean for funding police, fire, and schools, or what a higher sales tax would cost families on everything they buy. Until he does, it's a talking point, not a policy. That 20 percent exemption only applies to homesteads. It doesn't apply to commercial buildings, big box stores, warehouses, or corporate-owned land. On our $0.64 rate, a homeowner's real effective rate after the exemption works out to about $0.51 per $100 of value. A corporation with no homestead exemption pays the full $0.64 on every dollar. That's the actual design of this budget homeowners get real relief, and businesses and big corporations carry more of the load, not less. There's a difference between the seven of us and Representative Harrison worth pointing out too. You see us. At the grocery store, at your kids' games, at the restaurants around town, at the park. Some of us have our own kids out there playing in those same games and running around those same parks. You can walk up and tell us what's on your mind, and we sit across the table and work it out with you, because we live here. Here's the part that actually bothers me. Representative Harrison has attended zero of our council meetings. He has offered zero input on how to accomplish what he says he wants. He has my phone number. He has never once called or texted me to talk about any of this. Instead he picks a fight with us on Facebook and brands us the villains from a distance. I'd bet money that the next time he sees me and my wife at a public event, he'll walk up, shake my hand, and smile like we're old friends. That tells you what this actually is for him. Political theater, not principle.

If he actually wants to lower property taxes, he could file a bill next session to raise or remove it and let cities like Midlothian give homeowners real, lasting relief. That would take more than a Facebook post. Based on his record so far, I'd rather see it than expect it.
He also says he wants to eliminate property taxes altogether. That's not a plan, it's a slogan. Property taxes fund cities, counties, and schools. Getting rid of them means replacing billions of dollars in revenue with something else, and in every serious version of that conversation at the Capitol, that something else has meant a large increase in the state sales tax. Representative Harrison has never said what he'd replace that money with, what it would mean for funding police, fire, and schools, or what a higher sales tax would cost families on everything they buy. Until he does, it's a talking point, not a policy.
That 20 percent exemption only applies to homesteads. It doesn't apply to commercial buildings, big box stores, warehouses, or corporate-owned land. On our $0.64 rate, a homeowner's real effective rate after the exemption works out to about $0.51 per $100 of value. A corporation with no homestead exemption pays the full $0.64 on every dollar. That's the actual design of this budget homeowners get real relief, and businesses and big corporations carry more of the load, not less.
There's a difference between the seven of us and Representative Harrison worth pointing out too. You see us. At the grocery store, at your kids' games, at the restaurants around town, at the park. Some of us have our own kids out there playing in those same games and running around those same parks. You can walk up and tell us what's on your mind, and we sit across the table and work it out with you, because we live here.
Here's the part that actually bothers me. Representative Harrison has attended zero of our council meetings. He has offered zero input on how to accomplish what he says he wants. He has my phone number. He has never once called or texted me to talk about any of this. Instead he picks a fight with us on Facebook and brands us the villains from a distance. I'd bet money that the next time he sees me and my wife at a public event, he'll walk up, shake my hand, and smile like we're old friends. That tells you what this actually is for him. Political theater, not principle.

text:
Undocumented immigrants (often called illegal immigrants) have never been eligible for full federal health insurance programs such as Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare, or subsidized ACA Marketplace plans. This restriction has been in place since the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA).

They could still receive certain care through a handful of limited, legally required, or state-optional channels. These are the main ones.

Emergency rooms and Emergency Medicaid
Federal law (the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, or EMTALA) requires hospitals that accept Medicare to screen and stabilize anyone who comes to an emergency room with an emergency medical condition. Immigration status and ability to pay do not matter. Hospitals cannot turn people away from the ER for a true emergency.

If the person meets a state’s income and residency rules for Medicaid but is ineligible because of immigration status, the federal government can reimburse the hospital through “Emergency Medicaid.” This is not enrollment in Medicaid and does not give the person ongoing insurance. It only pays providers for treatment of the emergency condition (examples include labor and delivery, severe trauma, or, in some states, ongoing dialysis).

Emergency Medicaid spending has consistently been a small share of the overall Medicaid budget—less than 1 percent in recent years (around $3.8 billion, or 0.4 percent, in FY 2023). A large portion has gone to childbirth.

State-funded programs
A minority of states have used their own tax dollars (not federal Medicaid funds) to offer Medicaid-like coverage to some undocumented residents who meet income limits. Coverage has been most common for children. As of 2025–2026, roughly 14–15 states plus D.C. covered children regardless of status. Far fewer covered adults, and those programs were often limited by age, enrollment caps, or later scaled back because of cost.

Examples of states that offered some adult coverage at various points include California (Medi-Cal, later restricted new adult enrollment), Illinois and New York (mostly seniors), Oregon, Washington, Colorado, and Minnesota. Several of these programs faced enrollment freezes, benefit cuts, or new premiums by 2026.

These programs were paid for by state taxpayers, not the federal government.

Other access points
Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics) provide primary care on a sliding-fee scale based on income and generally serve people regardless of status.
Public-health services such as vaccinations and treatment of certain communicable diseases.
Hospital charity care or uncompensated care, where bills go unpaid and hospitals absorb the cost or shift it to other patients and payers.
U.S.-citizen children in mixed-status families can qualify for Medicaid or CHIP even if their parents cannot.

Undocumented adults have high uninsured rates (around 46 percent in recent survey data) and, on average, use less health care than U.S.-born citizens. They are typically younger and face barriers including cost, language, and fear of authorities.

In short, there was never a nationwide federal program giving undocumented immigrants comprehensive “free health insurance.” Access came mainly from the legal requirement that emergency rooms treat emergencies, limited federal reimbursement for those emergencies, state-only programs in a handful of states, and safety-net clinics or uncompensated hospital care. Recent federal and state policy changes in 2025–2026 tightened some of these channels further.

The facts you listed are mostly right. The United States did send a huge force to the Gulf in 1990–91, much of it based in Saudi Arabia after Iraq invaded Kuwait. Combined U.S. deaths in Desert Shield and Desert Storm were in the low hundreds (about 148 hostile deaths and more from accidents and other causes). Fifteen of the nineteen 9/11 hijackers were Saudi nationals. That is not in dispute.

What does not follow is the punchline: that “Saudi Arabia” received American protection and then showed no gratitude.

The Saudi *state* asked for that protection. King Fahd invited the coalition after Saddam seized Kuwait. Riyadh hosted the troops, joined the coalition, and treated the deployment as survival, not a favor it could later forget. The United States did not do this as charity. It was defending a major oil producer, the regional order, and its own strategic position after Iraq swallowed a neighboring state.

The hijackers were not the Saudi government. They were a small group of radicals, most of them young men recruited into al-Qaeda. Osama bin Laden — himself a Saudi who had already been stripped of citizenship — made the U.S. presence on the Arabian Peninsula one of his central grievances. He offered his own fighters to the royal family in 1990, was rejected, and then declared the monarchy apostate for inviting “Crusader” troops onto the land of the two holy mosques. Al-Qaeda was at war with the House of Saud as well as with Washington. Treating 15 murderers as the voice of the kingdom is the same mistake as treating Timothy McVeigh as “America.”

On the night of September 11 the Saudi government issued a public condemnation, offered condolences, and later expanded security cooperation — especially after al-Qaeda bombed compounds inside the kingdom in 2003. There are still serious, unresolved questions about private money, religious export, and whether some mid-level Saudis helped two of the hijackers after they arrived in California. Those questions are not the same as “the country we saved repaid us with 9/11.”

A government can be an ally, host half a million foreign troops, and still produce citizens who join a terrorist group that hates that alliance. That is ugly and worth examining. It is not a simple story of ingratitude.

text:
Sept. 11 widow blasts Saudis on anniversary of attacks: ‘How can it be 25 years and still we have no justice?’

Terry Strada, widow of 9/11 victim Tom Strada, shook up the ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks Friday by making a ringing denunciation of Saudi Arabia, the home nation of 15 of the 19 Al Qaeda hijackers who caused America’s darkest day.

Strada, whose husband was one of 658 Cantor Fitzgerald employees killed shortly after hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 slammed into the North Tower, asked aloud after reading Tom’s name: “How can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?”

Strada, the national chair of 9/11 Families United for Justice, argued that the US partner “fomented a rancid culture of anti-American terrorism around the globe and then sent its agents to support radical Islamist hijackers so they could attack you and all of our loved ones.”

“For 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families,” Strada continued as several spectators at the memorial service cheered.

“They broke promises, both public and private. It has been one betrayal after another,” added the widow.

The ceremony was attended by former Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden, who offered no visible reaction to Strada’s comments.

Recognizing Vice President JD Vance, who attended the ceremony on behalf of the Trump administration, Strada said: “Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction, that we have been suffering through.

“Vice President Vance, thank you for being here today,” she concluded. “Please carry that message back. Stand with the families. Stand with survivors. Stand with Americans. As my husband Tom would have said, that is always the right thing to do.”

Moments later, the nephew of another victim, Marsh & McLennan vice president Lisa Marie Terry, urged President Trump to “release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia while what’s left of the victims’ families are still alive.”

“For 25 years, the deep state has hidden the truth about what happened that day 25 years ago,” he said. “President Trump, you’re our last hope.”

Strada’s organization has pursued legal action for years that would hold the Kingdom liable for the attacks that killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and Shanksville, Pa.

Next month, a federal appeals panel in Manhattan will hear arguments focused on one shadowy figure, Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national who helped secure California lodging for a pair of American Airlines Flight 77 hijackers – but who left the country for the UK about a year before 9/11.

He was questioned at the request of the US and held by British authorities, but was never charged and eventually moved back to Saudi Arabia.

A 1999 video, unsealed by court order in 2024, shows al-Bayoumi – who had murky government ties, a web of official contacts, and who according to a 2017 FBI memo was on the payroll of Saudi intelligence – filming the US Capitol and talking about a “plan.”

Lawyers for the victims’ families say al-Bayoumi was “casing” the building – with 30 minutes of footage of the hour-long video focused on the iconic building’s entrances, showing its security procedures, and even its interior columns.

The 2004 9/11 Commission report concluded there was a high probability that the Capitol was the intended target of United Flight 93, which crashed in Pennsylvania.

Another video, from February 2000, shows a “welcome party” al-Bayoumi threw for the future hijackers, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar, soon after they moved to San Diego.

The Saudi government has long denied any role whatsoever in the planning of the attacks.

text:
WHO IS PAYING FOR A 6.76% MORTGAGE? PULTEGROUP $PHM IS:

The Growth Len5 is watching PulteGroup PHM at $118.18, +$1.77 / +1.52% today - eighteenth on that watch. The Atlanta company has built and sold houses since 1950, across 25 states.

The verdict: Pulte is selling more houses than it did a year ago and booking less money for them, and the entire difference is the discount it hands each buyer to make today's mortgage affordable.

Start with the rate, because it writes everything below. On Thursday, September 10, Freddie Mac published its weekly survey of what lenders across the country are quoting: the 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 6.76%, up from 6.71% the week before and 6.35% a year ago.

A buyer does not shop for a house. A buyer shops for a monthly payment. When the rate goes up, the same house costs more every month - and the builder makes up the difference.

Pulte does that mainly by pre-paying part of the buyer's interest, an arrangement called a rate buydown: the builder hands cash to the lender so the buyer's rate starts lower. It costs Pulte real money and never shows up as a lower price.

Here is the size of it. On July 22, for the three months to June 30, incentives ran 10.4% of the gross sale price, against 8.7% a year earlier. For a dollar figure: that 8.7% worked out to roughly $52,200 on a $600,000 house.

Now the two halves of that quarter, against each other:

- Net new orders 7,536 homes, +6% - first-time buyers +5%, move-up +4%, active adult +12%
- Homes sold but not yet delivered: 10,966, +2%
- What those homes are worth: $6.8B, -1%

More houses. Less money.

The profit line says it again. Home sale gross margin - the share of each sales dollar left after land, labour and materials - was 25.0%, against 27.0% a year earlier, though 0.6 of a point better than the March quarter.

- Home sale revenue $3.8B on 6,997 closings
- Net income $472M against $608M, -22%
- Profit $2.48 a share against $3.03, -18%, and ahead of the $2.38 expected

The gap between -22% and -18% is the buyback: $681M over six months on 5.5M of its own shares, about 3% of the company, so the profit divides across fewer of them. In the June quarter alone it paid $373M at an average $119.42 a share. It is $118.18 now - under what the company itself paid.

One company, six Len5es:

- GROWTH - PARTIAL, and the Len5 watching it. Wants profit growth the price has not already charged for. The price half is emphatic: about 11.9 times the last year of profit for a $22.2B builder with five straight profitable years behind it. The profit half is running backwards, which is exactly why it sits eighteenth rather than near the top - and the September quarter is modelled at $2.65 a share, roughly 10% under the same quarter last year. CHANGE IT: incentives easing back toward 8.7% while closings hold the 28,500 to 29,000 Pulte has reaffirmed for the year - what turns more houses back into more money.

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - NOT A FIT, and the nearest miss. Wants a sound business marked down after something visible and dated. The markdown is real but shallow: 18.2% under the $144.495 of February 17, and at 1.68 times book value - what would be left after selling up and paying every debt - it still costs more than its books say. No single dated event did this; the rate did it a week at a time. CHANGE IT: a fall to or through book value.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT. Wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, at a price short of its worth. The price is not the argument. Irreplaceable is: a buyer who dislikes Pulte's offer drives to the next subdivision, and four quarters of margin have shown who decides how much gets given away. CHANGE IT: that 25% holding through a full rate cycle instead of sagging with it.

- MOMENTUM - NOT A FIT. Wants a price at its best of the past year with the short climb and the long one agreeing. That best price is seven months old, and today's 1.5% has come on 542,627 shares so far against a 1.42M two-week average. CHANGE IT: a close back through $144.495 on real volume.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT, on size rather than safety. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners that the trade itself funds. Pulte returns plenty of cash; almost none arrives as a cheque. The dividend is $0.26 a quarter, $1.04 a year, about 0.88% here, against $2.48 earned in a single quarter. It goes ex-dividend Tuesday, September 15 and pays October 2. CHANGE IT: the dividend growing into the cash flow instead of the buyback taking all of it.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Founded 1950, and revenue this quarter is modelled about 6% smaller than last year's. CHANGE IT: nothing this business can do.

The same rate is not hurting everyone equally. Lennar at $79.79, +$1.89 / +2.43% today, the Miami builder, set its lowest price in a year yesterday at $76.63 and trades at 0.87 times book - under what its own land and houses are carried at, against Pulte's 1.68. Its quarter lands first, after Wednesday's close, with analysts modelling $1.30 a share against $2.00 a year ago, a fall about twice as steep as Pulte's. Lennar fits none of the six Len5es: below book is precisely the markdown Deep-Value hunts, but a profit expected to drop by a third is not the sound business that style needs behind the discount.

WATCH the incentive figure, 10.4% - not orders, not closings, not the share price. WHEN: Thursday, October 22, before the open, a date Pulte has set. RISK: the Federal Reserve decides Wednesday, September 16 at 2:00pm ET, and the live argument there is a rate RISE - which pushes mortgage rates up and the buydown bill with them.

A builder can hold its order book at almost any mortgage rate. It simply has to buy it, one buyer at a time. Pulte published that price on July 22 and publishes it again on October 22.

text:
Every young person now is reviling the Triple Lock and calling it out, rightfully, for what it is: a final, callous attempt by the older generations to pull up the ladder on the prosperity of yesteryear and live out their last days in splendour that is completely unimaginable to the average graduate today.

Yet we should not, at the same time, turn around and throw people out on their arses after a lifetime of honest work if we are going to extend the hand of welfare to the rest of our indigenous people. The suffering of any of our kin should alarm and aggrieve us - but how can we balance these needs? For opportunity for the youth, and care for the old?

This is one matter in which I think the Distributist approach stands triumphant - for the solution to the problem of pensions is not wholly financial, but largely cultural and social. For while we should be aiming to limit inflation by insulating our economy, breaking the private banks, and restricting currency printing; and we should be aiming to set out welfare provisions in some form, with greater investment in end-of-life care especially; the real answer to the care of he elderly is found in the familial structure of the past.

Our state pension began in 1908. Some companies offered their own throughout the 1800s. The Navy has offered them since 1700. But throughout those centuries of growing private and State provision of welfare, the main source of aid to those who needed it? It was local community, and family. 

If they did not live with you, then elderly parents lived close by; you could help them, and if you were indisposed for whatever reason, they had the whole village or the whole street who they knew, and who they could reach out to for support. They had their former employers, their local constables, their parish. Their first port-of-call was not the State, and nor should it be.

If we want to shoot for scrapping the Triple Lock and breaking the enslavement of the young to the old, one of our main considerations should be: how can we tie young and old back together again? How can we restore the nuclear and multi-generational family? How can we restore the community; the local support networkS, on which people used to rely? 

Our first instinct should not be to throw yet more taxes at the problem. It should be to address the underlying social rift that is exacerbating it.

🔥 Simple Guide to Starting Your Own Wyoming LLC ✅

You can do most of this yourself in an afternoon without paying thousands of dollars to lawyers or formation companies.

Here’s the basic process 👇

📍 1. Choose your LLC name

Make sure the name is available in Wyoming and includes LLC, Limited Liability Company or another permitted abbreviation.

Check availability through the Wyoming Secretary of State.

Cost: $0
Time: About 30 minutes

📍 2. Get a Wyoming Registered Agent

Every Wyoming LLC needs a registered agent with a physical address in Wyoming.

If you qualify to act as your own registered agent, you can do it yourself.

For most people living overseas, it is much easier to simply pay a registered agent.

A basic service can cost as little as $25 per year.

📍 3. File your Articles of Organization

This officially creates your Wyoming LLC.

Wyoming state filing fee: $100

You can file directly with the Wyoming Secretary of State.

Time: Usually less than an hour to complete the application yourself.

📍 4. Create an Operating Agreement

This sets out who owns the company, how it operates and what happens in different situations.

Wyoming doesn’t require you to file it with the state, but you should still have one.

You can create a simple one yourself or pay someone to prepare it.

Cost: $0 if DIY.

📍 5. Get your EIN

Your EIN is basically the company’s federal tax identification number.

The IRS does not charge you for an EIN.

If your principal place of business is in the United States, you may be able to apply online.

If you’re living overseas and your principal place of business is outside the U.S., international applicants generally need to apply by phone, fax or mail instead.

Cost: $0 if you do it yourself.

That’s basically it.

A Wyoming LLC does not need to cost thousands of dollars to establish.

For people who don’t want to do the paperwork themselves, there are inexpensive formation companies that will handle most of it.

Friends of ours use:

https://t.co/ii4VtdvG1y

They currently advertise Wyoming LLC formation for around $153 total, including their formation service, state filing costs and registered agent, with registered agent service currently $25/year afterward.

Another option:

https://t.co/UWmSAnzTeQ

They offer LLC formation, registered agent and additional structuring services if you want more help rather than doing everything yourself.

Always check their current package pricing before signing up because services and fees change.

And remember:

The LLC is simply the business vehicle. It isn’t automatically a tax loophole.

Where you live, where you perform the work, your citizenship and your personal tax residency can all matter.

For many non-Americans running an international online or service business, however, a simple U.S. LLC combined with the right personal residency and tax setup can be an excellent starting structure.

Start simple.

Add complexity when you actually need it.

@CoffindafferFBI  The information is two teams competed in three eras in stopping communism in Indonesia 1952-1958. Some were split between both teams seeing which might work or if they might work together. Team Nixon the first team was concerned after 1949 that Indonesia might fall to Chinese influenced communists. Typical "Executive Action" / "Flexible Response" was to be used and was used to funnel war supplies secretly to military leaders the US supported in Indonesia. This could be a very bloody plan. Team JFK wanted to win popular support from Indonesia by helping labor and farming to become product in free market economies in the Western style. This plan of supporting farmer and small business was what the British were NOT doing in Ireland over many years. In this JFK team was James and Glorian Donegan, Duke Edward, Marilyn Monroe, the Rockefeller family, the Von Trapp family, some Catholic entities and maybe the Vatican, Malcomn X, Dr. King, and Robert F. Kennedy. Those on the JFK team tried to support Sukarno as an alternative to Suharto, but Suharto began to fail in leadership. He had been tough to win over. With that plan now a failure in 1963 the next plan was to reveal the Nixon plans the US DOD still had underway in Indonesia and elsewhere, but the team formed under V.P. Nixon was still intact. Ultimately all on the JFK team were eventually "silenced."

The documentary record supports several important foundations of this model. The Eisenhower administration considered supporting anti-Sukarno regional forces in 1958, despite recognizing that the confrontation could produce civil war. Memorandum by Director of Central Intelligence Dulles, January 31, 1958 and Foreign Relations of the United States: Indonesia, 1958–1960. Kennedy subsequently discussed Indonesia’s Eight-Year Economic Development Plan and offered American help in examining and supporting it. Memorandum of Conversation concerning Indonesia’s development plan and Briefing material concerning Sukarno and economic-development assistance. After the 1965 crisis, American policy moved toward supporting anti-communist Army officers and eventually the Suharto government. Memorandum Prepared for the 303 Committee and Report on Suharto’s New Order.

Written version
Ed Donegan proposes that two overlapping American coalitions competed over how to prevent Indonesia from entering the communist bloc. The first, described as Team Nixon, emerged during the Eisenhower–Nixon years. It treated communist influence primarily as a security problem and relied upon covert action, military relationships, secret deliveries of weapons and support for anti-Sukarno forces. The CIA-backed regional rebellion of 1958 represents the clearest documented example of this approach. Because the strategy encouraged armed conflict within Indonesia, it carried an inherent possibility of extensive bloodshed.

The second coalition, described as Team JFK, sought to compete with communism by making a Western-oriented economy attractive to ordinary Indonesians. Its proposed instruments included agricultural productivity, organized labor, education, small businesses, international development and cultural engagement. Donegan compares this approach with the economic opportunities that Britain historically failed to provide adequately to Irish farmers and working people.

The distinction should not be presented as an absolute division between two formal organizations. Kennedy inherited the CIA, Pentagon and Indonesian military relationships established under earlier administrations. His government pursued economic development and personal diplomacy with Sukarno while also maintaining military-assistance and anti-communist programs. Some participants may therefore have crossed between the two strategies or supported a combination of them.

In Donegan’s interpretation, the wider JFK-associated network included James and Glorian Donegan, Marilyn Monroe, members of the Rockefeller and Von Trapp families, Catholic organizations and possibly the Vatican, Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr., Robert F. Kennedy and Duke Edward. Their inclusion is part of Donegan’s broader thesis; it is not presently established that these people constituted a coordinated historical “team.” Each proposed member will need an evidence entry explaining the person’s connection, activity, date and source.

Donegan further argues that this network initially considered Sukarno a possible alternative to Suharto but lost confidence in him by 1963. Suharto in did gain power starting in late 1965.

Finally, Donegan argues that, after the development strategy failed, members of the JFK-associated network intended to expose the covert military system still operating in Indonesia and elsewhere. He connects their subsequent deaths, removal from influence or inability to speak publicly with the preservation of that system. Rather than saying simply that “all were silenced,” the finished presentation should contain a separate chronology for each individual. That will allow readers to distinguish documented death or suppression, evidence of intended disclosure, and Donegan’s inference that the events were connected.

For the graphic, I recommend three vertical panels, one for each era, with a blue development path for Team JFK, a red covert-military path for Team Nixon, and a central purple area showing people or policies that crossed between them. This would make the interaction clearer than depicting two entirely isolated camps.

ChatGPT The clearest form is a three-era table followed by a written explanation. The overall period should probably be 1952–1968, because the argument continues well beyond 1958.

text:
In the time before time, when the world was still new and the two leggeds had not yet walked upon it, the Creator called the animal nations together.
They came from every direction. Salmon rose from the deep rivers. Buffalo thundered in from the open plains. Eagle dropped from the high sky. Bear, Wolf, Deer, Turtle, and all the rest gathered in a great circle and waited.
The Creator spoke.
“I am going to send a new being among you,” He said. “This being will be called Human. He will be clever and restless. He will walk upright and reach for things beyond his grasp. I will give him a great gift so that he may find his way in the world. The gift is knowledge. The gift is truth. The gift is the understanding of who he is and why he is here.
“But I will not place it where he can stumble upon it without effort. He must search. He must earn it. Tell me, my children where shall I hide this gift?”
Salmon spoke first.
“Give it to me, Creator. I will carry it to the deepest part of the deepest ocean. No one will ever find it there.”
The Creator shook His head.
“One day Human will learn to travel even the floor of the sea. He will find it too soon.”
Buffalo stepped forward, heavy and sure.
“Let me take it to the very center of the Great Plains, far from every trail. The grass will hide it.”
Again the Creator refused.
“Human will cover the earth. He will walk every plain. He will find it there as well.”
Eagle opened his wings.
“Then I will fly it to the moon,” he said. “No living thing can reach that far.”
The Creator smiled, but His answer was the same.
“Even the moon will not be far enough. One day Human will stand there too.”
One after another the animals offered their hiding places the highest mountain, the darkest cave, the farthest forest. Each time the Creator said no. Human would go everywhere.
The circle fell quiet.
Then the smallest voice rose from the ground.
It was Mole.
Mole lived beneath the earth. Long ago he had given up the use of his eyes, yet he had learned another way of seeing. He saw with the heart.
“I know the place,” Mole said.
Everyone leaned in.
“Hide it inside them,” Mole whispered. “Place the gift in their own hearts. Then only those who are willing to look inward only the wisest and the bravest and the most honest will ever find it.”
The Creator was silent for a long moment.
Then He nodded.
“Yes,” He said. “That is the only place Human will not think to look first. And that is the only place worth finding.”
So it was done.

AN OHIO MAN HAS BEEN SENTENCED AFTER ATTEMPTING TO BRIBE AN UNDERCOVER OFFICER WITH SPRITE AND CHICKEN ALFREDO

AKRON, OHIO — Gregory Palowski, 34, was sentenced Thursday after allegedly attempting to bribe an undercover officer during a traffic stop by offering a two-liter bottle of Sprite and a still-warm container of chicken alfredo he'd just picked up from a nearby restaurant.

Court records say the offer was made with complete sincerity and zero hesitation.

Court documents state Palowski slid the alfredo container across the console "still steaming" before the officer even asked for license and registration
Witnesses say he specifically emphasized the Sprite was "the good two-liter, not the store brand"
He allegedly told the officer "there's enough for two, if your partner's hungry too"
Court records show he attempted to sweeten the offer by including a plastic fork already in the bag
The officer reportedly had to decline twice before Palowski accepted that the bribe wasn't landing
Prosecutors say the entire exchange was captured clearly on the officer's body camera, alfredo steam and all

The arresting officer reportedly noted in his report that the pasta "did smell genuinely good" but was logged into evidence regardless.

"In sixteen years on the bench, I've seen bribery attempts with cash, favors, even property, but never a home-style pasta dish," said Judge Harold Vance, a 16-year veteran of the Summit County Court.

The Sprite and alfredo were both logged as evidence. Neither was returned.

He offered dinner instead of documents.
The court still served him something else entirely.

text:
Medical technology is going to seem near-miraculous soon. 

Lab grown human nerves can now fire at real sensory nerve speeds.

Researchers at Rice University and ETH Zurich built a 3D system in which human sensory neurons and Schwann cells form working myelin, the insulating sheath that lets signals travel quickly. Grown in hydrogels that feel more like living tissue than plastic dishes, the nerves survived more than 100 days. 

Electrical recordings showed conduction velocities in the same range as human sensory nerves, and those speeds increased when myelin formed.

The point is not just that the wrapping looks right under a microscope. The insulation actually changes how the nerves communicate.

Why it matters: 

Multiple sclerosis attacks myelin in the brain and spinal cord, slowing or blocking nerve signals. This platform uses Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerves rather than the central nervous system, so it is not a complete MS model yet. 

What it does offer is a way to watch myelin form, get damaged, and — the next test — recover, while measuring whether signal speed returns. The same 3D approach can be adapted with oligodendrocytes and brain-like tissue to study remyelination therapies for MS more directly.

📸 Rice University

text:
From @grok

DNA is the weakest part of the case, not the proof. Nobody serious treats a spit kit as a deed to the slave trade.

Commercial tests estimate continental ancestry against modern reference samples. Those labels shift when the company updates its model. That is a product change, not a court finding. Plenty of White Americans show a few percent African ancestry; plenty of Black Americans show European ancestry. That is what four centuries of the same country produced. It does not identify a named enslaved person in Alabama in 1840, and it does not create a blood-quantum tribe.

Paper does the work DNA cannot: 1870 census → parents on a death certificate → Freedmen’s Bureau or an estate inventory. When that chain exists, it is ordinary genealogy. When it does not, you do not get to fill the gap with a percentage on a website.

So the jab is half right: DNA-as-membership is sloppy. The error is thinking that is the only method on offer, or that mixed ancestry makes every lineage claim fake. Mixed blood is common. A documented ancestor is still a documented ancestor.

text:
Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information issue. It’s on each of us to change that. With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.  Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. 

The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.  So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.  This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.  You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.  Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty 

1. He made the border a real border again.  In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.  

2. He reversed mass migration. America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 were forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.” Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.  

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act  and required the detention of criminal illegal aliens. Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.  Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.  

4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years. According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.  This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.  Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle 

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.  Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.  

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the "one" was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.  Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.  

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments. That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America. No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.  

8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.  

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade. Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.  

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America. Once the world’s largest energy importer “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export well over 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year. Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.  

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year. For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.  Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.  Trump Made Elections Matter Again 

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.  Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”. Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.  

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s precisely what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017. In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.  

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.  Trump terminated it completely and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?  

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years. From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats are paid to resist the voters.  What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees "worked" from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”  

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government. Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.  He Defended Faith and Family 

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges who overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.  Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.  He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.  No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.  

18. He got men out of women’s sports and restored biological reality to federal policy. The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.  Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.  

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.  That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.  

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination. Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.  He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First 

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.  Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.  

22. He drove China out of the Caribbean. China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.  Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.  

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.  

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population. Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.  Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.  25. He restored the warrior ethos  and reversed the recruiting crisis. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.  Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.  Now Act Like It Matters Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 

25: I could give you hundreds more.  Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.  And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that "news" happens to be.  Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them.  This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.  So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.  Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.  Because it does.

Excerpt from my book regarding September 11, 2001: 
Earlier that year, 2001, we began a new project for Prevacid working on a revamped arrangement of “Great Balls of Fire” with Jimmy Hall as lead vocalist. Stylishly, for lack of a better description, it was a big band sound with some Jerry Lee Lewis influence, obviously. The project required months of production before it was finally approved. The video featured highly detailed, time-intensive animation that portrayed the interior of a stomach consumed by the flames of heartburn. The stomach lining was rendered as a city on fire, with fire trucks and firefighters working to extinguish the burning buildings.
The Prevacid commercial was scheduled to premiere in September 2001. The moment I saw the devastation of 9/11 and considered the world beyond that tragedy I knew, we all knew, the spot could not and should not air. Ten months of work were scrapped, and rightly so.
On a personal note, In August of 2001 my wife and I were planning our Honeymoon in Paris. I asked Miles to book our  roundtrip tickets. Miles did so, but I asked him to change the tickets and reroute. I can't remember why, but I said, "I don't want to fly Osama Bin Ladin Airlines. I don't think I'd ever uttered that name before. I have no idea why I said that. Miles changed the tickets. We were to fly out from Boston and back the same way and instead we flew out of St Louis and back to St. Louis. On September 11, my bride Stephanie and I flew back from our belated honeymoon in Paris, France. A day earlier, by mistake, we left our hotel and checked in at Charles de Gaulle Airport for our flight home. A lady at the ticket counter caught our mistake and convinced us to go back to our hotel to enjoy another day in Paris. We spent another beautiful day in Paris and then left for America the next day, September 11. About halfway through our flight, the captain came on the speaker and said, “I have some very disturbing news to tell you. The World Trade Center and the Pentagon in Washington D. C. have been attacked.” With all North American airspace closed, they routed our flight to Gander, Newfoundland. We spent 26 hours on the tarmac, with no food or water, watching plane after plane land one at a time. Ten thousand people landed in a town of 11,000 residents. About a hundred of us, including the flight crew, were driven by a school bus to a small Masonic Lodge. School bus drivers were on strike, but made an exception that day. We slept on the floor, on cots, and in chairs. Stephanie and I slept on the top floor of the lodge, with two small bathrooms for one hundred men and women. Everyone was in shock. Some were crying, some were speechless. We had one landline to call home. No cell towers. The people of Gander were fabulous. They opened their homes to us. The mayor and his wife came to the lodge and offered their home to anyone who wanted a place to shower. Everyone just stood there looking at them. The room was quiet. No one spoke up but Stephanie and I. They took us to their home for showers and a breakfast. Later, the mayor gave us a tour of Gander. It was majestic. He also took us to the site of the tragic 1985 aviation disaster that killed 248 soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division and eight crew members. I instantly thought, that may have been better to see on another day, but it was part of their history. The mayor and I traded emails and stayed in touch for years. Gander was our refuge for four and a half days. Within three years, I was tasked with developing the budget for a music video to be created as a tribute for the families of service members who lost their lives in the War on Terror.

Saudi Arabia reportedly asked Trump for help against the Houthis. Twice.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Donald Trump twice on Thursday, urging the US to launch immediate strikes against Houthi forces in Yemen.

Trump refused.

According to US officials, Washington has no plans for now to enter another direct war with the Houthis. The preferred option is intelligence, coordination and support for Saudi Arabia — without opening yet another American front.

The problem is that the front has effectively arrived at Bab el-Mandeb anyway.

Saudi Arabia wants airstrikes. Pakistan wants everyone to calm down. Trump apparently wants one thing above all: not another war.

Why should anyone in Europe care about some island off Yemen?

First answer: you probably don’t.

Second answer: look at the price at the pump.

Third answer: look at Russia.

Iran is putting pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important oil arteries. Saudi Arabia can partly bypass Hormuz by pumping crude across the kingdom toward the Red Sea.

But at the other end of that escape route are now the Houthis.

They have pushed toward Mocha and Dhubab and reportedly taken Perim, the small island sitting directly inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

If shipping through Bab el-Mandeb becomes too dangerous, vessels have to go around Africa. That means thousands of extra kilometres, more fuel, more time, higher insurance premiums — and ultimately higher prices.

Oil is already above $100. US diesel has crossed $6. Europe gets more expensive energy and transport.

And then Russia enters the conversation with the most predictable sales pitch imaginable:

“We have cheap oil and gas.”

Soon after come European politicians arguing that perhaps sanctions have gone too far and perhaps Russian energy should return. In Germany, that argument is increasingly associated with the AfD.

So the chain is remarkably simple:

Iran squeezes Hormuz → Houthis squeeze Bab el-Mandeb → oil and shipping costs rise → voters see bigger bills → Russia offers cheaper energy → European radicals ask voters to forget why Europe stopped buying it in the first place.

That is why Perim — a tiny island roughly the size of Manhattan — may suddenly be much closer to Berlin and Warsaw than it looks on a map.

In geopolitics, distance is sometimes measured not in kilometres, but in the price of a barrel of oil.

text:
Dr @ShashiTharoor articulates India should treat a deeper, structured partnership with Europe as a core tool of strategic autonomy — not as a replacement for the US, but as a hedge against an unpredictable Washington and a coercive China.
Tharoor’s argument is that mid-2020s geopolitics has made the old US-centric bet fragile. Tariffs, energy-policy pressure, and sudden swings in American policy have injected volatility into a relationship that once felt structurally predictable. Multi-alignment is therefore no longer optional: Quad, Gulf, Singapore, and others matter, but the EU is the missing large, high-capacity partner.
The January 2025 India–EU FTA (“mother of all deals”) is the economic pillar — 2 billion consumers, roughly a quarter of world GDP, tariffs cut or eliminated on ~96% of goods, plus rules on services, digital trade, and tech. For India it is a buffer against protectionism and a premium market; for Europe it is the flagship of “China Plus One” diversification.
The security pillar is the new Security and Defence Partnership: maritime and cyber cooperation, counter-terrorism, AI, access to Europe’s €150 billion defence initiative, joint production, and technology transfer. Europe cannot match US military or financial hegemony, but it offers what the US currently does not: institutional stability, technological depth, and policy predictability. Shared concern over Chinese coercion in sea lanes and connectivity projects makes the fit practical, not merely rhetorical.
Thus true autonomy is not isolation or passive non-alignment. It is active, overlapping, high-value partnerships. Binding India’s economic future to the FTA and its security architecture to Europe creates a double hedge — against Chinese assertiveness in the neighbourhood and against erratic American engagement. Two large democracies, in this reading, can become an anchor of a rules-based order when both great-power alternatives look less reliable.

(September 9, 2022) Fort Myers, Florida -  Authorities ID victim of alleged serial killer suspected in ‘Fort Myers 8’ case

Florida authorities working with genetic genealogists have identified one of eight serial killer victims whose skeletal remains were found in the Fort Myers woods in March 2007.

Robert Ronald “Bobbie” Soden is the fourth of the “Fort Myers Eight” to be identified. The other four men remain listed as John Does.

Authorities believe alleged serial killer Daniel Owen Conahan Jr. is responsible for the deaths of Soden and the other seven men, as well as several murders in Charlotte County known as the “Hog Trail murders.” Conahan, 68, has been in prison since 1996, when he was arrested for the kidnapping and murder of Richard Allen Montgomery.

The U.S. Navy veteran and former Punta Gorda licensed practical nurse is on death row at Union Correctional Institution in Raiford. Though he is suspected of at least four other murders in Charlotte County, he has never been tried in any of those cases.

Conahan has proclaimed his innocence in each of the murders.

According to a Fort Myers police spokesperson, Soden’s identification is the result of Fort Myers cold case detectives’ work with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and Parabon Nanolabs, a Virginia-based lab that offers forensic genealogy services to law enforcement agencies.

Genealogists were able to build a family tree for Soden, previously known only as Victim H, based upon DNA extracted from his remains.

DID YOU KNOW ABOUT THIS: AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED.
 
A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants
who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the
children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.
 
There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who
would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to
bundle them into carriers and strollers.
 
Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they
needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran
back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well,
here we are, on our own."
 
About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.
Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up
toddlers.
 
The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of
the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .
 
Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped
in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the
cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the
Old West.
 
Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from
wandering off. Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter
around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until
the parents could be notified and come get their children.
 
The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on
any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men
there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.
 
The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted;
could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories
from the Pentagon.
 
It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life,
liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It's the military who salutes the
flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.

text:
Remembering Betty Ann Ong.

She grew up in San Francisco’s Chinatown, the youngest of four, the kid who used to watch planes take off at SFO and later made flying her life. 

Friends called her Bee. 

She collected Beanie Babies, visited seniors in Boston on her days off, and picked up extra trips so she could afford a vacation with her sister. 

On September 11, 2001, that extra trip put her on American Airlines Flight 11.

She was not supposed to be on that plane. 

From the rear galley she picked up an Airfone and became the first person to tell the ground what was happening: the cockpit would not answer, people had been stabbed, the cabin was filling with something that made it hard to breathe. 

“I think we’re getting hijacked,” she said. 

Then she stayed on the line for 23 minutes. 

She gave seat numbers. 

She answered questions. 

Near the end she asked them to pray.

That call was the first confirmed warning that the country was under attack. 

It helped controllers begin clearing the sky. 

The 9/11 Commission later called her a hero. 

A recreation center in her old neighborhood now carries her name.

She was 45. 

She was doing her job until the last second. 

Today is a good day to say her name.

text:
KC @ BOS has one of the clearer starter + incentive gaps on the board.

Boston enters 80-67 and still fighting for AL playoff positioning. Kansas City is 65-82 and playing out the year, while Boston has intentionally lined up Sonny Gray → Ranger Suárez → Payton Tolle, which looks a lot like the beginning of an October rotation structure.

That matters because Boston needs to bank this type of home series before the schedule gets tougher.

The Statcast matchup is where it gets interesting.

Seth Lugo:
17.4% K
18.4% Whiff
25.1% Chase
.279 xBA allowed
.344 xwOBA
.452 xSLG

He isn’t missing enough bats right now, which is dangerous against a Boston lineup with several patient/contact hitters:

Roman Anthony — .355 xwOBA / 13.7% BB
Mickey Gasper — .370 / 12.8%
Wilyer Abreu — .350 / 10.7%
Adley Rutschman — .337 / 10.0%

Lugo has also allowed 6+ hits in five straight starts, so the concern isn’t just surface ERA — the contact profile is showing up in the results too.

Sonny Gray gives Boston the cleaner run-prevention profile:

22.1% K
6.5% BB
33.1% Chase
.297 xwOBA
.373 xSLG
46.9% GB

One thing I’m NOT forcing is Gray’s strikeout over.

KC has too much contact through Bobby Witt Jr., Pasquantino, Massey, Perez and Loftin. Gray can pitch six strong innings without necessarily getting to 6+ Ks.

Narrative-wise, KC still has individual motivation. Witt remains one of the best young stars in baseball, Jac Caglianone brings legitimate power, and Carter Jensen is riding strong recent form. So this isn’t “Boston wins because KC doesn’t care.”

The actual handicap is:

Better starter
Better bullpen setup
More team-level incentive
More lineup patience
Better contact environment against Lugo
And a price structure where Boston -1.5 offers much more value than simply laying nearly -200

Clean script: Gray controls KC while Boston consistently puts balls in play against Lugo and creates separation.

Danger script: Lugo’s deep pitch mix creates weak early-count contact and Boston wins something like 4-3 instead of covering.
