Breaking News
Bombshell CIA 9/11 files lay bare Bill Clinton's horrific Bin Laden mistake...as ex-president grimly faces families at Ground Zero

Bill Clinton's White House was warned that Osama bin Laden wanted to crash a bomb-packed plane into an American city three years before the hijackers struck, explosive CIA files reveal.

The warning was a part of a September 10, 1998 report prepared for senior Clinton officials cleared to read the then-president's most secret morning intelligence digest, according to the Wall Street Journal. 

Headlined 'Bin Laden's Location and Intentions,' it offered no date or target, but made clear the terror chief had Washington, DC, in his sights. Bin Laden's terrorists would crash an airplane into the Pentagon three years later. 

Other papers show analysts told the White House in July 1998 that a bin Laden strike on the US was 'plausible,' and in October 2000 that he remained 'committed' to hitting American targets, though spies 'cannot pinpoint targets or timing.' 

The revelation surfaced as Clinton was at Ground Zero for the 25th anniversary, standing among the very families whose loved ones died in the attack the memo foreshadowed.

In 2001, bin Laden was featured in at least 18 separate editions of Bush's daily intelligence digest, seven of them landing on the former president's desk weeks before the towers fell.

One July 24, 2001 memo even flagged that an 'expected imminent' bin Laden operation had been postponed, while cautioning that other attacks could still be in motion. 

The 71 documents were released by the CIA to mark a quarter-century since nearly 3,000 people were murdered in New York City, the Pentagon and in a Pennsylvania field. 

The 9/11 Commission had mentioned the 1998 memo, but never disclosed it had been written for the president's own briefing stream.

Former acting CIA chief Michael Morell told the Wall Street Journal that the documents prove the agency delivered 'long and loud strategic warnings' that two administrations failed to act upon.

But agency insiders told the outlet that the intelligence at the time was often thin and drawn from 'highly questionable sources.' 

The lack of certainty, insiders told WSJ, made it difficult for policymakers to respond to a potential plot with no time, place or method.

However, one CIA analyst claimed that counterterrorism operations were not a presidential priority before 9/11, and the agency lacked the manpower to dismantle bin Laden's terror network. 

Bin Laden had played a key role in the 1998 embassy bombings in East Africa and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole.

text:
NEBRASKA OFFERS AN IMPORTANT CONTRAST

Oregon is not the only Medicaid-expansion state subject to the new federal requirements.
Nebraska also expanded Medicaid and is subject to H.R. 1. Yet Nebraska became the first state in the nation to implement the new Medicaid work requirements, beginning May 1 — eight months ahead of the federal deadline — integrating the requirements into its existing eligibility and renewal system. The dramatically different experiences deserve examination.

“If H.R. 1 alone explains Oregon's crisis, then we should expect other Medicaid-expansion states operating under the same federal law to face the same crisis,” Diehlsaid. “Nebraska's experience gives us good reason to ask a different question: What did Oregon do differently?”

Diehl said Oregon should use the federal changes as an opportunity to confront the problems that existed before H.R. 1 — including inadequate provider reimbursement, rapidly growing public health care expenditures, regulatory costs and barriers to new health care capacity, and continued expansion of taxpayer-funded coverage.

“We absolutely should protect a strong safety net for Oregonians who truly depend on it,” Diehl said. “But a sustainable safety net requires discipline. We can't continually expand who and what taxpayers are expected to cover, make care more expensive to deliver, restrict new capacity, underpay the providers actually delivering the care, and then blame Washington when the numbers don't work.”

“Oregon's health care crisis was already here. H.R. 1 didn't create it. If we're serious about fixing it, Salem needs to start taking responsibility for the decisions Salem made.”

Dear members of the American press!

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device. I've developed a concept based on the opposite principle: the device should adapt to the user and interact with them as naturally as possible.

I believe this technology has the potential to be the next major step in the development of consumer electronics. It offers a fundamentally new way to interact with the digital environment and has the potential to replace many existing devices that accompany people in their daily lives today.

If my assessment is correct, this isn't just another gadget, but a platform capable of transforming the market in the same way that the personal computer, iPod, and iPhone once did. Such opportunities arise extremely rarely, and that's why they deserve independent attention and objective assessment.

I believe Apple has the experience, engineering culture, and vision necessary to turn this idea into a world-class product. Moreover, the successful implementation of such technology could strengthen the leadership of the American tech industry at a time when global competition is becoming increasingly fierce.

I'm not asking you to take my word for it. I'm asking only one thing: help draw Apple's attention to this development and give it the opportunity to be considered by those capable of objectively assessing its potential.

If the technology truly represents the value I see in it, ignoring it could be a missed opportunity. If not, that will become clear after a professional evaluation. But in either case, the idea deserves to be heard.

Thank you for your attention.

Sincerely,

Alexander.

I’ve been holding $SURPLUS for 3 months now, and it’s not for no reason.

The fact that this coin has remained standing, and even thrived, through all the liquidity rotations we’ve seen over the past few months, on a not-so-hot chain, should tell you something.
It is my absolute conviction that onchain utility gems like these are the new altcoins of this cycle that will go on to produce the 100-1000x winners of this golden 
bull run.

Come now, lemme simplify the tech real quick to give you an idea of exact tech and utility here.

Excess. Leftovers. SURPLUS?
That’s right. That’s exactly what the $Surplus is all about.

A lot of people and companies buy AI power in advance.
They pay for large ChatGPT/Claude/OpenAI API credit packages upfront, or buy monthly and yearly subscriptions that give them a certain amount of usage.

But here’s the problem:

These prepaid credits can go unused and when they expire, that leftover value simply disappears.
The money is gone.

The AI capacity goes unused.
Instead of letting all of that go to  waste, $Surplus creates a marketplace where sellers can sell their leftover AI capacity to buyers at discounted rates.
Sellers win because the alternative is letting that capacity expire.

Buyers win because they get cheaper AI inference.

Think of it like a farmers’ market for produce that would otherwise go to waste.

The farmer recovers some value.
The buyer gets cheap produce.
And as AI gets more expensive and usage continues exploding, there’s potentially a huge market for unused AI capacity.

But why is $SURPLUS special?

$Surplus tackles this in 3 distinctive ways:

1. Safe
Solving the problem 
Surplus acts as a secure middleman between buyers and sellers.

Your prompts and data stay hidden from individual sellers.
You only have to trust Surplus, rather than some random provider.

2.Fair and open
Solving the marketplace problem 
Surplus works like an open order book, with multiple sellers competing for buyers.
The same model can be offered at different prices, with buyers routed to the cheapest healthy provider.
Real competition. No single seller gets to dictate the market.

3.Easy
Solving the infrastructure problem 
Normally, accessing different AI models means juggling different providers, API keys and integrations.$Surplus gives you one simple API, compatible with the way you already use AI APIs.
Change the base URL, and you can access hundreds of models through one connection.

Safe. Fair. Easy.

And then there's the team behind $Surplus which is another reason I'm super bullish.
An 8-member lean team, including some unpaid/equity contributors.
The team lead, Mac @mac_eth , has previously worked at Coinbase/Base and has experience at Square/Cash App, along with a data science and early-project background, which is very valuable for a project like this.

Top-tier team + real product with live usage, real sellers, listed capacity, real buyers, routing requests and measurable savings (40-60% discounts) =a 9 fig project.
I don’t make the rules

$Surplus

text:
My 9/11 story
(lightly updated version of a blog post I wrote in 2016 for the 15th anniversary)

In September 2001, I was the young co-founder of a NYC tech startup, TripleHop Technologies.   

We were building enterprise search software, using whatever AI existed at the time, building what would be today close to what a Glean does.  

We had maybe 25 people on the team at the time.  Pretty much all of us were at the very begining of our careers, barely out of school, unexperienced, but highly enthusiastic.

Our office was located on the 53rd floor of the North Tower at the World Trade Center.

We had ended up at the World Trade Center fairly randomly.  Our first office was located on Water Street, right above a 24 hour McDonald’s.  It looked more like a decrepit apartment than an actual office, occasionally didn’t smell that great, but it was cheap and good enough.

But after a year or so, the team had grown, and that office had become too small, so we started looking for a bigger one.

At the time, for a reason or another, there wasn’t a lot of office inventory on the market in the area where we wanted to be.  

We looked for a bit, couldn’t find anything suitable, until one of us had the strange idea of inquiring at the World Trade Center, which felt like a long shot. 

Turned out that the World Trade Center had some smaller offices, and some availability.  In those dot-com bubble days, they also were quite eager to attract young tech startups, and were willing to offer us some preferential terms. 

So we went to take a look, and visited two offices in the North Tower. 

One was a large office at the very top of the building, perhaps the 104th floor, I don’t exactly recall. It had unbelievable views, but it really felt like taking that office would be pushing it – even with a good deal, we were just a little seed-funded startup, after all. Also, the elevator ride took forever. 

So instead we chose the smaller, cheaper office on the 53rd floor.  

We really liked our new office, and the World Trade Center in general.  It felt like a little town, with a lot of retail and amenities below the surface, and its own subway station. We ate a bit too often at a Sbarro joint located right outside the ground floor elevator.

The night before 9/11, my co-founder Renaud Laplanche and I worked very late into the evening, as we did most nights.  In true nerdy founder fashion, we played a ping pong game or two, as we did pretty much every time before calling it a night – the ping pong table being our attempt at creating a startup culture.  

I left, and think Renaud may have stayed on that night to finish working on a proposal for a prospective customer.

The morning after, when the plane hit the North Tower at 8:46am, I was home, about to leave for work.   

Like many young tech people, we were night owls but not early birds, typically showing up at the office around 9:30am.  

I had the TV on, and as about to turn it off and walk out of the door, saw the “breaking news” scroll at the bottom of the screen mentioning a plane collision, but no image.    

As I had a faraway view of the World Trade Center from the window of my West Village studio apartment, I looked up and saw what seemed like a little bit of smoke at the top.

I assumed the plane that had hit the tower was a small tourist plane.  We would often see them fly by the office, above the nearby Hudson River, often at altitudes that felt very close to us.  It had crossed my mind more than once that it wouldn’t take that much for one of them to hit the tower by accident.

Then, like so many others, I saw those unbelievable images on TV. I called my family back in France.  Shortly thereafter, phone lines went down. 

The rest of the day was surreal and gut-wrenching, although I remember feeling mostly numb.

I went on a mad scramble to see if everyone at TripleHop was ok. For many hours, we just didn’t know.  With no phone working, we accounted for most people via email, but a number did not reply for a while.

It eventually turned out only one person from the team, Kenton Beerman, was at the office at 8:46am.   He made it out shocked but unscathed.

Perhaps as a way to cope psychologically, or just because they were amazing people, I remember that the team was incredibly focused on saving the business that day.  

This was obviously pre-AWS, we had our own server room in our office, but thankfully our CTO Joaquin Delgado and his team had backed everything up.  By the end of the day, we were essentially back up and running.

After a few days, we found shared office space.  But business didn’t go back to usual. In addition to everything else, 9/11 was the final nail in the coffin for the economy after the dot com bubble burst.  The next couple of years were a complete nuclear winter.

Thankfully, we had raised a $5M Series A (a solid amount at hte time!) a few months before 9/11, which kept us afloat.  We also managed to win a few deals in Europe, which gave us a bit more cash.  

Eventually business picked up strongly in late 2003 and 2004, potential acquirers came knocking, and TripleHop was acquired by Oracle in 2005.

We all went on with our lives.  My co-founder Renaud reached extraordinary entrepreneurial success and defined a whole new industry.

We all have families now.  I occasionally see pictures of beautiful children on my Facebook feed.  

I rarely talk about 9/11, and have tried to not think about it too much. 

It took me a very long time to go visit the 9/11 memorial downtown.  

I finally made it just a few weeks ago, after a board meeting nearby, walking there almost by accident.

Looking at the names engraved in the marble, I was reminded that it wouldn’t have taken much.  An hour later, a few floors lower. Or choosing that office on the 104th floor instead of the other one, a few months prior.

And I feel deeply connected not just to those names, but to New York. 

Before 9/11, New York felt like an exciting, but ultimately foreign, city. After 9/11, I truly started feeling like a New Yorker.  

Everyone remembers where they were on 9/11.  Everyone has a story of some sort, many infinitely more tragic.  

This is just mine.

Hey @MaxNiederman: 

I'm one of those founders you're talking about. I raised for a crypto infra company, it worked at first and then it went nowhere, then I spent 2y too long chasing something that wasn't working specifically because I was afraid of what "other people would think"

I'm not qualified to talk about what "other founders in this situation" would do (nor do I care to) but I sure am qualified to talk about myself and my company and my experience and I will say that it's been way way harder than you're making it sound.

LPs invest in VC because they want alternate asset exposure. 
VCs invest in early stage tech companies b/c they want excess return.

So that means your job is to at *least* exceed SPY perofrmance over the term of your company. But venture is power laws, so your job is to figure out how to make something happen that's a statistical anamoly.

My investors have been incredibly supportive, and if I could rewind a few years with the one biggest lesson I've learned in the last few years, it would be to ignore that voice in my head that sounds like what you're saying.

Either way, no hard feelings, but just wanted to offer a different perspective.

A Shooting Star forms after an uptrend when buyers push price aggressively higher, but sellers step in and reject the move, forcing price back toward the session lows.

Look for a small real body near the bottom, little/no lower wick, and an upper wick ideally 2–3X the body.

→ Bulls had control
→ Buyers attempted another push higher
→ Sellers absorbed the demand
→ Price was rejected
→ Momentum may be shifting to the bears

But remember:

A Shooting Star is a SIGNAL candle, not automatically an ENTRY candle.

5 RULES FOR YOUR TRADING PLAN

→ LOCATION MATTERS: Look for Shooting Stars after an established move higher, especially at horizontal resistance, trendlines, major moving averages, Fibonacci levels or supply zones.

→ WAIT FOR CONFIRMATION: Don’t automatically short the candle. A close below the Shooting Star’s low provides stronger evidence of a bearish pivot.

Signal → Confirmation → Entry

→ DEFINE INVALIDATION: The Shooting Star high provides a logical invalidation level. If price breaks and holds above it, the bearish thesis is weakening.

→ LOOK FOR CONFLUENCE: Resistance, bearish momentum, overextended RSI, MACD weakness, volume rejection or trendline resistance can increase the quality of the setup.

→ CHECK RISK/REWARD: Identify support before entering. If significant support sits immediately below your entry, the trade may not offer enough downside to justify the risk.

STATISTICS MOST TRADERS DON’T KNOW

→ Thomas Bulkowski’s historical testing found the Shooting Star produced a bearish reversal about 59% of the time on daily charts, showing why blindly shorting the candle isn’t enough.

→ It ranked 55th out of 103 candlestick patterns in his overall performance ranking.

→ Context matters. Candlestick patterns tend to become more useful when combined with trend, location, confirmation and proper risk management.

Professional candlestick trading isn’t:

“Shooting Star → SHORT.”

It’s:

Trend → Location → Signal → Confirmation → Risk/Reward → Execution

The candle creates the setup.

Price confirmation creates the trade.

The reason is simple. Cybersecurity is an enormous real-time inference problem. Modern security platforms ingest staggering volumes of endpoint, identity, cloud and network events. AI must correlate signals across multiple systems, determine whether activity is benign or malicious, select a response and act before an attacker can exfiltrate data, encrypt another machine or move laterally through the organization.

Cerebras CISO Naor Penso explains the requirement clearly:

“There is no viable way for AI to be adopted into that ecosystem if it’s not in real time.”

“Every minute counts.”

“Real time is critical for cybersecurity…and for AI it is really important to have fast inference in order to hit that real-time mark.”

This is exactly where Cerebras’s architecture becomes strategically valuable. Security investigations increasingly require multi-agent systems. One agent analyzes network activity. Another examines endpoint behavior. Others check identity, cloud logs, historical patterns and threat intelligence. Their conclusions then feed into a larger reasoning model that determines whether the event is benign, requires human review or demands immediate action.

Every sequential model call adds latency. Penso explains that with conventional inference, a complex chain of agents can turn a single investigation into “30 seconds, a minute, two minutes or three minutes” before reaching a resolution.

In cybersecurity, those minutes have consequences.

“Every minute is another few hundreds of megabytes of data that could have left the organization.”

“Every minute that is passing by with ransomware running in the environment is another minute, another computer getting infected.”

Fast inference therefore affects far more than chatbot responsiveness. It determines whether sophisticated AI reasoning can operate inside the window in which a cyberattack can still be stopped.

Cerebras can allow security platforms to deploy larger, more capable models and networks of specialized agents while preserving real-time performance. That creates the possibility of deeper investigation, higher-quality conclusions and faster automated response.

Penso describes the advantage:

“With fast inference, you’re getting hyper-fast speeds of responses across all your agents and still not caving in on the quality.”

That is the importance of the $CRWD partnership.

CrowdStrike is using Cerebras technology, while Cerebras has selected CrowdStrike as its cybersecurity platform. This is a reciprocal commercial and technical relationship between a leading AI inference company and one of the world’s leading cybersecurity platforms.

Penso says CrowdStrike recognizes the same architectural requirement:

“CrowdStrike sees exactly what we believe is true, which is fast inference is imperative for the success of cybersecurity.”

He summarizes the partnership this way:

“We’re providing the fastest inference on earth and the highest quality as well…and CrowdStrike delivers the best endpoint security in the world.”

CrowdStrike gives Cerebras a powerful real-world validation point. Falcon operates at immense scale, where latency, throughput and response quality directly affect the product. If Cerebras can help CrowdStrike reason across its security data faster, respond to threats sooner and make Charlotte AI more capable, this partnership could become a showcase for Cerebras across the entire cybersecurity industry.

Other vendors face the same problem. Palo Alto Networks, SentinelOne, Microsoft, Zscaler, Cloudflare and countless security startups all want increasingly autonomous AI agents. Those agents must investigate threats, query multiple tools and generate reliable answers almost instantly.

The competitive question may become: How intelligent can your security platform be while remaining genuinely real time?

That is a hardware and inference problem, and Cerebras was built specifically to solve it. The long-term opportunity extends beyond one CrowdStrike deployment. Cerebras could become an inference layer beneath AI-driven detection, investigation and response across the cybersecurity industry.

Penso’s conclusion captures the urgency:

“If we as security practitioners don’t adopt AI, we will be breached very fast.”

“AI is today, in my mind, the only viable way for us to scale.”

Attackers are using AI to increase their speed, sophistication and targeting. Defenders will need AI systems capable of reasoning and responding at machine speed. Cerebras offers the rare combination of model intelligence, massive throughput and extremely low latency that this transition requires.

Cybersecurity is becoming an AI inference race.

CrowdStrike choosing Cerebras suggests that Cerebras intends to be the engine helping the defenders win it.

💰 At the 2021 Cyber Symposium, Mike Lindell claimed he had data proving China hacked the 2020 election. He offered $5 million to anyone who could prove that data was not real election data. Robert Zeidman, a computer expert and Trump supporter, took up the challenge.

Zeidman submitted a report arguing that the data "unequivocally does not contain packet data of any kind and do[es] not contain any information related to the November 2020 election."

A 2023 arbitration panel ordered Lindell to pay Zeidman the $5 million. Lindell challenged the award in court. A federal judge in Minnesota upheld the ruling in 2024.

An appeals court overturned the ruling in July 2025; the judges said the arbitrators looked beyond the strict wording of the contest rules when they made their decision. In January 2026, the Supreme Court refused to hear Zeidman's appeal.

Current status: in August 2026, a federal judge sent the case back to the same arbitration panel for a new decision. This time the panel must stick only to the exact wording of the contest rules, nothing else.

Zeidman won the arbitration in 2023. Whether that legally entitles him to the $5 million is still being decided.

Thank you Grok, prepare a short draft for Americans to draft that can be used to petition representation to protect the 1st and 14th amendments. Use all that apply: 

Religious Liberty

First Amendment: 

Prohibits Congress from making any law respecting the establishment of a religion (Establishment Clause) or prohibiting the free exercise thereof (Free Exercise Clause). [1] (https://t.co/K42dsLb7cP)

No Religious Test Clause (Article VI): 

Bans any religious test as a qualification for holding any public office or trust under the United States. [1] (https://t.co/5uOzlqpc34)

Private Property

Fifth Amendment: States that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, and prohibits private property from being taken for public use without just compensation (the Takings Clause).

Fourth Amendment: Protects people against unreasonable searches and seizures, ensuring privacy and security in their homes and private property.

Third Amendment: Restricts the government from forcing citizens to quarter soldiers in their private homes during peacetime.

Fourteenth Amendment: Extends these due process and property protections to apply against state governments, ensuring states cannot deprive any person of property without due process of law.

Note: The right to gather peacefully for public worship is protected by the First Amendment, which explicitly combines religious liberty and peaceful assembly.

When public worship takes place in a peaceful manner, it is shielded by three intersecting parts of the First Amendment:

1. The Right to Peaceful Assembly Public Gatherings: This clause guarantees the right of people to gather peacefully in public spaces (like parks, sidewalks, and streets) for any lawful purpose, including religious services or vigils.

2. The Free Exercise Clause Public Worship: This protects the right of individuals and groups to practice their faith publicly. The Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled that religious exercise includes not just belief, but physical acts of worship, assembly, and speech in public forums.

3. The Freedom of Speech Religious Expression: Public worship, prayer, and proselytizing are recognized forms of speech. The government cannot ban religious speech in public spaces if it allows other forms of expression (like political protests or community events) in those same areas.

Cite relevant case rulings as well: Several landmark Supreme Court decisions have established the precedent that religious expression (including public worship, prayer, and proselytizing) is protected speech, and that the government cannot exclude religious voices from spaces opened to other types of expression. [1]

The fundamental precedent is the Public Forum Doctrine, which states that once the government opens a forum for public debate or expression, it cannot engage in "viewpoint discrimination" by locking out religious groups. [2]

The critical "case files" that built this legal foundation include:

1. Widmar v. Vincent (1981)

The Case: A public university in Missouri allowed registered student organizations to use its facilities for meetings, but banned a student group from using those spaces for religious worship and discussion. [3]

The Precedent: The Supreme Court ruled that the university had created a public forum and could not exclude the student group based purely on the religious content of their speech. The Court held that religious worship and discussion are fully protected forms of speech under the First Amendment. [3, 4]

2. Lamb’s Chapel v. Center Moriches Union Free School District (1993)

The Case: A New York school district permitted social, civic, and recreational groups to use school property after hours, but denied a church permission to show a film series about family values from a religious perspective. [1]

The Precedent: The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that the school district violated the Free Speech Clause. The Court declared that enforcing a ban on religious points of view while permitting secular ones is unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. [1]

3. Rosenberger v. University of Virginia (1995)

The Case: The university funded various student-run publications using student activity fees but refused to fund Wide Awake, a magazine that offered a Christian perspective on student life.

The Precedent: The Court ruled against the university, clarifying that the government does not violate the Establishment Clause by providing a neutral benefit (like funding or meeting spaces) to a broad class of groups, even if some of those groups have a religious message. Denying the funding based on the magazine's religious viewpoint was a violation of free speech. [5, 6]

4. Good News Club v. Milford Central School (2001)

The Case: A public school in New York allowed residents to use the building after hours for community events. A private Christian club for children requested space to sing songs, read Bible stories, and memorize scripture, but was denied.

The Precedent: The Supreme Court held that the school had established a "limited public forum". Because the school permitted other groups to teach morals and character development to children, it could not bar a group from doing the same thing simply because they approached the topic from a religious perspective. [2, 7]

5. Shurtleff v. City of Boston (2022)

The Case: The City of Boston allowed private community groups to fly flags of their choosing outside City Hall. However, the city denied a request from a Christian organization to fly a "Christian flag".

The Precedent: The Supreme Court ruled unanimously that flying the flag was a form of private expression, not government speech. Because Boston opened its flagpole as a forum to anyone who asked, it could not exclude a flag solely because it contained religious imagery. [8]
